Verify shell, streaming, and hydration behavior in browser tests

questions.prompt: Match each rendering concern to its review focus.
questions.explanation: Each boundary has a different operational consequence for data access, bundle size, and loading behavior.

questions.prompt: Which route is the best candidate for a static shell plus streamed dynamic section?
questions.explanation: Partial prerendering works well when stable shell content can appear while a smaller request-time section resolves.

options.label: A product page with stable content and a personalized inventory panel.
An admin route where every section depends on per-user permissions.
A fully client-side canvas game with no server data.

questions.prompt: Order the debugging path when a route unexpectedly becomes runtime-bound.
questions.explanation: Find the runtime source, narrow the boundary, and test the visible outcome.

items.label: Locate request-time API or uncached data access
Decide whether only a subtree needs runtime work
Wrap the runtime subtree with a meaningful Suspense fallback
Test the shell and delayed content on mobile

questions.prompt: Starting from items = [], a click queues [A], then its timer calls setItems(items.map(...)). What array does that captured map read?
questions.explanation: The callback keeps the render’s empty array, so mapping it returns []. A later timer does not refresh a closure. useState supplies a value and a setter; neither the captured array nor the setter result is a Promise for future state.

options.label: The empty array from the render that created the handler.
The latest committed array, because the timer runs later.
A Promise that resolves to the next state.

questions.prompt: Which change preserves independently added items when asynchronous completions arrive out of order?
questions.explanation: Each dependent write must build on pending state, and each completion must target its own item ID. A later stale replacement can undo a correct append. Waiting longer does not change the captured array or establish an ordering policy.

options.label: Use functional updates for both appending and updating the matching item ID.
Fix only the append, then replace the array captured by each callback.
Make the timeout long enough for every render to finish.

questions.prompt: Why does await setItems(next) fail to make the old handler read the new items value?
questions.explanation: Calling a setter from async code is valid. Its return value is not a Promise that waits for a commit, and await does not replace the handler’s captured variables. It also does not freeze React rendering; calculate dependent state with a pure updater.

options.label: The setter does not return a commit Promise, and this handler keeps its render snapshot.
React setters cannot be called from async functions.
await freezes React rendering until the component unmounts.

questions.prompt: Where should a request run when its result updates an item?
questions.explanation: Perform I/O outside the updater, then calculate the next state synchronously. An async updater returns a Promise instead of an array. A synchronous updater with I/O is still impure: development Strict Mode can invoke updaters twice, so it cannot promise one request.

options.label: Outside the state updater; await it, then queue a pure update by ID.
Inside an async updater passed to setItems.
Inside a synchronous updater so it runs exactly once.

questions.prompt: Two requests edit the same item. The newer result arrives first. Do functional updates alone stop the older response from overwriting it?
questions.explanation: Functional updates receive pending state but do not infer which request is authoritative. Responses are not sorted by start time. An item ID identifies the target; a request revision distinguishes competing operations for that target.

options.label: No. Use a per-item request revision or serialize writes according to the chosen policy.
Yes. Functional updates sort responses by request start time.
Yes. Using an item ID makes every response for that ID current.

questions.prompt: A timeout has already started awaiting a request when Clear items is clicked. What prevents its late response from affecting a new list?
questions.explanation: A generation guard rejects the old operation’s result locally. clearTimeout cannot stop an already-running callback. Abort can reduce unnecessary work when supported, but it is not proof that the server rolled back or never committed a mutation.

options.label: Invalidate its generation and check that generation before applying the result.
Only call clearTimeout on the timer that already fired.
Assume aborting the client request rolls back any server write.

exercises.title: RTK Query Cache Identity and Invalidation Checkpoint

questions.prompt: The final subscriber leaves at t=40s with keepUnusedDataFor: 60. No one returns. When is eviction expected?
questions.explanation: Unused retention starts when the subscription count reaches zero. It is not measured from fetch time, and cache eviction does not require a mutation.

options.label: Around t=100s, because retention starts after the final unsubscribe.
At t=60s measured from the original request.
Never, because only mutations remove query entries.

questions.prompt: Deleting a record on page one shifts page three, which never provided that record tag. What helps?
questions.explanation: A collection dependency covers membership/count changes outside a visible page. An unprovided entity tag will not match that page, and longer retention cannot correct stale membership.

options.label: Invalidate only the deleted record ID, which always matches all pages.
Increase keepUnusedDataFor so the stale page lives longer.
Invalidate a scoped collection or PARTIAL-LIST tag as well as relevant entity tags.

questions.prompt: Tenant changes affect only prepareHeaders; the endpoint arguments stay equal. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Headers are not automatically default key dimensions. Model non-secret identity scope and clear protected state on transition; random keys waste reuse and fail to express the actual data contract.

options.label: A random number in every argument to disable all reuse.
Explicit cache scope and account-transition cleanup for identity-dependent data.
Nothing: all request headers automatically enter the default key.

questions.prompt: A matching tag is invalidated for an entry with no active subscribers. What normally happens?
questions.explanation: Invalidation removes unused matches and refetches subscribed matches. Tags neither force background fetches for every unused entry nor automatically merge mutation data into query responses.

options.label: The unused matching entry is removed.
It must immediately refetch despite having no subscribers.
Its JSON data is automatically patched from the mutation result.

questions.prompt: A mutation succeeds but delayed invalidation never runs while a queryFn stays pending. What should you inspect?
questions.explanation: RTK 2.x delayed invalidation waits for pending work to settle. Styling cannot unblock the lifecycle, and matching tag names in separate API slices do not share invalidation.

options.label: Only CSS, because a successful mutation guarantees immediate refresh.
Whether the same string tag exists in a different API slice.
Pending work and the API invalidation policy; make the query lifecycle settle appropriately.

questions.prompt: Why should an empty author list still provide a collection tag?
questions.explanation: An empty result is still a cached server projection that can become stale after creation. Tags do not change endpoint type and do not provide global entity normalization.

options.label: Because collection tags globally normalize all author objects.
A later create can invalidate the cached empty collection.
Because an empty list otherwise becomes a mutation.

exercises.title: RTK Query Foundations and Request Ownership Checkpoint

questions.prompt: Two panels call getAuthor with the same ID in the same API/store. What should happen?
questions.explanation: The endpoint and serialized argument identify the entry, so concurrent subscribers share it. Hook count does not require duplicate HTTP calls, and React element keys do not define RTK cache identity.

options.label: They share the cache entry and an in-flight request.
Each hook must always make a separate request.
They share data only if both panels have the same React key.

questions.prompt: Switching author A to B must not show A while B loads. Which hook field fits?
questions.explanation: currentData belongs to the current argument. data may retain a previous argument result; copying it once creates a stale second owner and does not protect identity changes.

options.label: data always contains only the current argument result.
Copy data into local state once and ignore later updates.
currentData, with explicit loading and error handling for B.

questions.prompt: Where should an unsaved multi-step editing draft live?
questions.explanation: Drafts have a different owner and lifetime from server snapshots. Directly mutating cached results breaks the state contract; Redux Toolkit can model client workflows with ordinary slices.

options.label: Only on the server, because Redux Toolkit cannot hold client state.
In intentional client state with its own save/reset and persistence policy.
Always inside the RTK query response object by direct mutation.

questions.prompt: An author ID is optional until selection. What avoids an invalid query without conditional hooks?
questions.explanation: skipToken expresses a skipped typed argument while preserving hook order. Conditional hooks violate React rules, and fake IDs create avoidable errors and misleading cache entries.

options.label: Pass id ?? skipToken to the query hook.
Call the query hook only inside an if block.
Pass an empty ID and rely on the server to reject it.

questions.prompt: A background refresh starts while valid current data is visible. What UI is usually suitable?
questions.explanation: isFetching includes background work; preserving useful current data avoids disruptive flicker. Hiding all failures conceals staleness, while unconditional spinners discard a useful result.

options.label: Always replace all content with a full-screen spinner.
Hide every error because cached data exists.
Keep the data, show updating state, and expose refresh errors.

questions.prompt: A POST endpoint performs an idempotent search without changing server state. Which endpoint type can fit?
questions.explanation: A query can use POST for read semantics and cache by its argument. HTTP method alone does not mandate mutation, and fetchBaseQuery supports methods beyond GET.

options.label: Neither: RTK Query supports GET requests only.
A query, because operation semantics matter more than the HTTP verb.
A mutation is mandatory for every POST.

exercises.title: RTK Query Mock Interview and Code Review Checkpoint

questions.prompt: A review finds stale spinners and cross-account cached data. What is the strongest first priority?
questions.explanation: Cross-account display requires urgent scope correction and regression coverage. Animation changes cannot fix data isolation, and server authorization remains mandatory regardless of cache keys.

options.label: Fix and test identity boundaries while preserving server authorization.
Treat cache keys as a complete replacement for authorization.

questions.prompt: Invalidation triggers an HTTP request, but its response contains old data. What next?
questions.explanation: An observed request narrows the problem. Old response data points upstream; if response data is correct, inspect client selection. Broad repeated invalidation is not a diagnosis.

options.label: Assume no request occurred because the UI is stale.
Invalidate every API forever without inspecting the response.
Inspect server consistency and HTTP/cache layers, then selectors if the response is correct.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks about a newer RTK API. Which answer shows useful judgment?
questions.explanation: A concrete mechanism and product tradeoff demonstrate understanding. Version recitation alone is weak, and modern API support does not validate an application’s custom persistence path.

options.label: Claim every modern API automatically repairs legacy persisted state.
Explain infinite query page identity and the scroll consequences of collapsing a refetch to one page.
State the version number without describing any behavior.

questions.prompt: A patch passes tests but deployment has not been observed. What can you report?
questions.explanation: Tests support code behavior in the tested environment, not deployment or impact conclusions. Customer recovery and absence of data loss require separate evidence.

options.label: Code and test validation passed; deployment and customer recovery remain unverified.
No data loss occurred because the tests are green.

questions.prompt: Which design best separates offline data from execution state?
questions.explanation: Durable snapshots need identity and schema policy; commands need idempotency/reconciliation. Internal cache state is not a stable domain database, and automatic replay can duplicate writes.

options.label: Persist all internal query/mutation fields forever as the only offline database.
Replay every pending mutation whenever the app launches.
Versioned account-scoped snapshots plus explicit refresh and a separate durable command policy if needed.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a strong senior answer from naming API methods?
questions.explanation: Senior judgment connects mechanisms to evidence and boundaries. Compilation cannot prove lifecycle correctness, and a version bump cannot substitute for an incident-specific reproduction and recovery policy.

options.label: Recommend the newest version as the answer to every incident.
State the invariant, failure case, tradeoff, test, and remaining uncertainty.
Guarantee correctness whenever the code compiles.

exercises.title: RTK Query Modern APIs and Version Traps Checkpoint

questions.prompt: An infinite feed varies by tenant and topic and navigates using a cursor. How should it be modeled?
questions.explanation: The collection identity stays stable across pages while the page parameter advances. Dropping tenant/topic creates collisions, and per-page API slices fragment subscriptions and invalidation.

options.label: Tenant/topic in queryArg; cursor in pageParam.
Only the cursor in queryArg; tenant/topic are never cache dimensions.
A new API slice for every fetched page.

questions.prompt: Which version first added Standard Schema validation to RTK Query?
questions.explanation: Standard Schema support arrived in 2.7.0. The case-study 2.2.8 baseline predates it; 2.12.0 includes later fixes and improvements rather than introducing the original schema API.

options.label: RTK 2.12.0 was the first version with any endpoint schemas.

questions.prompt: In RTK 2.11+, what does refetchCachedPages: false do on an infinite-query refetch?
questions.explanation: The option collapses the retained window to one refreshed page. It does not preserve all later pages and does not disable the endpoint; scroll behavior needs an explicit product policy.

options.label: Disables every future request for this endpoint.
Refetches the first cached page and shrinks the retained cache to one page.
Refreshes the first page and keeps all remaining cached pages unchanged.

questions.prompt: Schema validation fails and normal endpoint error behavior is desired. What converts the failure?
questions.explanation: catchSchemaFailure performs conversion. onSchemaFailure is a notification hook; casting a payload neither validates it nor changes the runtime error path.

options.label: catchSchemaFailure returning the base query error shape.
onSchemaFailure alone always converts it into a handled error.
A TypeScript assertion on the response payload.

questions.prompt: How should the modern cancellation behavior be described?
questions.explanation: Modern RTK ties automatic abort to entry removal. Shared subscriptions and retention can keep work alive; even a transport abort cannot prove rollback of a remote write.

options.label: Every component unmount immediately cancels every shared request.
Aborting a request guarantees the server transaction was rolled back.
Cache-entry removal can abort pending work; one subscriber unmount is not always removal.

questions.prompt: A response is transformed before caching. Which schema validates the wire shape first?
questions.explanation: rawResponseSchema validates before transformResponse; responseSchema validates the final result. skipSchemaValidation disables checks and is not a stricter validation mode.

options.label: skipSchemaValidation validates the raw shape more strictly.
responseSchema always validates only the original wire shape.

exercises.title: RTK Query Mutations and Error Recovery Checkpoint

questions.prompt: A save handler uses await trigger(args) then always shows Saved. A handled 400 still shows success. What fixes the flow?
questions.explanation: Handled errors can be returned in the trigger result; unwrap exposes promise-style rejection. fixedCacheKey shares mutation state and does not alter HTTP error semantics.

options.label: Use unwrap with try/catch, or inspect the returned error result explicitly.
Assume every handled RTK error already rejects the ordinary trigger promise.
Set fixedCacheKey so HTTP errors become thrown exceptions.

questions.prompt: Edit one patches A to B, edit two patches C, then edit one fails. Why is naive undo risky?
questions.explanation: Inverse patches describe local changes, not distributed write ordering. Immer cannot order server operations, and an older patch does not automatically account for later success.

options.label: Immer automatically orders all server writes by user intent.
An inverse patch always knows which later request succeeded.
The earlier inverse patch can overwrite newer intent; serialize or reconcile with server state.

questions.prompt: updateQueryData targets an endpoint/argument with no cached entry. What happens?
questions.explanation: updateQueryData targets an existing exact entry and does not initiate a fetch or patch by tags. upsertQueryData is the explicit creation/replacement mechanism.

options.label: It patches every entry with a matching tag.
It does not create the missing entry; deliberate upsert may be needed.
It automatically starts a GET and creates the result.

questions.prompt: Five requests return 401 together. What is a sensible reauthentication design?
questions.explanation: Single-flight refresh prevents a stampede and needs session/race cleanup. Recursive unbounded refresh can loop; a 403 usually requires permission handling rather than repeated token refresh.

options.label: Coordinate one refresh, retry within a bound, and prevent stale-session credentials from being applied.
Recursively call the refresh wrapper on every 401 without a limit.
Retry every 403 as a token expiry indefinitely.

questions.prompt: A purchase times out after the server may have committed. What is safe?
questions.explanation: A client timeout cannot prove server rollback. Idempotency and reconciliation must be server contracts; fixedCacheKey only controls shared local mutation result state.

options.label: Assume timeout guarantees rollback and retry with a new operation ID.
Use fixedCacheKey as the server idempotency token automatically.
Use server idempotency and a reconciliation/status contract before retrying ambiguously.

questions.prompt: A custom baseQuery catches a network exception. Which result preserves failure semantics?
questions.explanation: A handled error keeps failure visible and supports predictable endpoint lifecycles. Empty data hides outages as valid results, while uncaught expected exceptions bypass the intended base query contract.

options.label: Throw every expected transport error without a declared error contract.
Return a typed error result for the UI and lifecycle to handle.
Return an empty data array so callers see success.

exercises.title: RTK Query Persistence and the Loading Incident Checkpoint

questions.prompt: After process death, a raw persisted pending entry returns but no request exists. What explains the loader?
questions.explanation: Serialized pending state does not recreate a promise or prove server activity. The thunk can reject a duplicate initiation for that key even when the original client request no longer exists.

options.label: Restored execution metadata can block initiation without restoring the actual request.
Every restart automatically recreates the original fetch promise.
A pending entry proves that the server is still computing the request.

questions.prompt: Which statement about RTK 2.2.8 and 2.12.0 rehydration is accurate?
questions.explanation: The inspected dedicated reducers skip pending entries in both versions. Generic state restoration is a separate path, and upgrading alone cannot guarantee the correctness of custom persistence wiring.

options.label: Every RTK rehydration path always restores pending entries.
Installing 2.12.0 repairs every custom persistence reconciler automatically.
Their dedicated extractRehydrationInfo reducer path filters pending entries; raw state restoration can bypass it.

questions.prompt: Why filter pending records both before writing and after reading old storage?
questions.explanation: Both directions cover distinct populations: future snapshots and existing installations. A write filter does not itself migrate old data; a read repair does not prevent malformed snapshots from being written.

options.label: Reading alone proves future versions never persist pending records.
Writes prevent recurrence; reads repair already persisted bad entries.
Writing alone guarantees existing disk data is immediately migrated.

questions.prompt: The app has unsynced drafts alongside a broken API cache. What repair is preferable?
questions.explanation: Drafts may be irreplaceable. A scoped migration can repair regenerable cache without erasing them; deleting unrelated data neither explains nor fixes the pending lifecycle defect.

options.label: A targeted versioned cache repair that preserves unrelated durable data.
A blanket storage purge because all Redux state is disposable.
Delete the draft slice to reduce the number of cached queries.

questions.prompt: Which regression best proves the forever-loading repair?
questions.explanation: The real restore and request path must progress. A refetch invocation may be blocked by the thunk, and a mocked successful hook bypasses the defect entirely.

options.label: Assert only that refetch was called.
Mock the query hook to return successful data.
Restore through the real config, subscribe, observe a new fake request, and reach data or error UI.

questions.prompt: A restored pending purchase marker is removed. What follows?
questions.explanation: The local marker cannot establish the remote outcome. Both automatic replay and assumed success can be wrong; durable command IDs and server status/idempotency are needed.

options.label: Mark the purchase successful because pending implies eventual success.
Reconcile the server operation; removing local state does not justify replay.
Automatically resubmit the purchase because removal proves it never committed.

exercises.title: RTK Query Production Architecture and Testing Checkpoint

questions.prompt: Two feature files need coordinated Author invalidation. What is the usual starting point?
questions.explanation: Endpoint injection preserves the shared cache/tag namespace. Equal tag names across separate APIs do not coordinate them, and duplicate middleware registration is not required.

options.label: Inject endpoints into a shared base API and register its middleware once.
Create unrelated API slices with equal tag names and assume cross-slice invalidation.
Register the same API middleware once per screen.

questions.prompt: selectFromResult returns a newly filtered array each time. Why can rerenders persist?
questions.explanation: The returned fields are compared shallowly. A fresh nested array changes a field reference; a new outer object with stable fields is expected, and real selected changes must still rerender.

options.label: The outer result object is forbidden from being newly allocated.
selectFromResult guarantees no component ever rerenders.
The selected array reference changes; memoize derived collections or select stable values.

questions.prompt: Which lifecycle is suitable for a stream tied to cached data?
questions.explanation: Cache-entry lifecycle work can own a stream and clean it up. Render-driven sockets leak/duplicate work; a permanently pending HTTP query confuses query completion and can delay invalidation.

options.label: Keep the HTTP queryFn unresolved forever to represent socket lifetime.
onCacheEntryAdded with validated events and cleanup after cacheEntryRemoved.
Open a new socket in every render and never close it.

questions.prompt: What avoids sharing one visitor’s Redux state with another in Next.js?
questions.explanation: A server-global store can leak request state. Follow request-safe boundaries and server/client ownership; cache keys are not authorization and must not contain tokens.

options.label: Request-safe store/provider boundaries and client-owned RTK Query usage.
A server-global mutable Redux store reused for all requests.
Move access tokens into serializable query keys to authorize server rendering.

questions.prompt: Why might refetchOnFocus work on web but not on React Native?
questions.explanation: Browser listener defaults do not supply native AppState/connectivity integration. RTK can run in native apps, and cache retention settings do not create lifecycle events.

options.label: RTK Query supports only desktop web.
Increasing keepUnusedDataFor emits native focus events.
Native lifecycle/connectivity signals need appropriate custom listener integration.

questions.prompt: Which setup can prove tag invalidation actually refetches?
questions.explanation: A real store exercises endpoint arguments, middleware, subscriptions, and tags. Mocked hook data or import assertions bypass the mechanism and cannot prove refetch behavior.

options.label: Assert the component imported a hook with the right name.
A real configured store with controlled transport and assertions on requests and final data.
Mock every query hook to return the expected post-mutation response.

questions.prompt: What sound does the small circle add to the h-row?
questions.explanation: Handakuten is the small circle that changes h-row kana to p-row sounds.

options.label: A p sound, as in ぱ pa
A b sound, as in ば ba
A g sound, as in が ga

questions.prompt: Which spelling reads kitte, stamp, with a held consonant?
questions.explanation: Small っ holds the following t sound; it is not pronounced as a full tsu.

questions.prompt: Why does きょう begin with kyo rather than ki-yo?
questions.explanation: Small ょ contracts with the preceding i-row kana, so きょ is one contracted sound kyo.

options.label: ょ is small and combines with き.
き is followed by small っ.

questions.prompt: Which word has the long a sound in obaasan, grandmother?
questions.explanation: The extra あ extends the a sound. おばさん without it means aunt.

questions.prompt: Put the beginner decoding checks in a useful order.

exercises.title: Product Engineering Durable Jobs and Revenue Safety Checkpoint

questions.prompt: A provider finished an export; the worker crashed before recording success. What is the safest retry plan?
questions.explanation: Redelivery proves the message needs handling, not that the external effect failed. Reconcile a stable operation identity where supported. Otherwise keep the uncertainty explicit; neither blind retries nor invented success preserve correctness.

options.label: Reconcile via a stable provider key or operation ID before repeating the effect.
Always generate again because the queue redelivered.
Mark success without checking whether an output exists.

questions.prompt: The API writes a job, then crashes before publishing its queue message. Which design closes this gap?
questions.explanation: An atomic job/reservation/outbox transaction leaves durable dispatch intent after a crash. Publishing first can create work without an accepted job or reservation. A tab cannot preserve the backend acceptance contract.

options.label: Publish first and assume the database write will succeed.
Keep the queue message only in the browser tab.
Commit the job, credit reservation, and outbox record atomically.

questions.prompt: Two workspaces reuse the same idempotency key. What is the correct boundary?
questions.explanation: Tenant scope prevents unrelated requests colliding or leaking results. A body fingerprint detects changed requests under the same key. Prompt text omits workspace, input revision, model, and configuration identity.

options.label: Scope the key to the workspace and compare the request fingerprint.
Use one global key namespace and return the first workspace’s result.

questions.prompt: Worker A pauses, its lease expires, and worker B commits success. A resumes. What protects the result?
questions.explanation: A lease can expire while its previous holder is still running. The commit must validate attempt ownership and state/version, so stale workers cannot overwrite B. Last-write-wins is unsafe for results and ledger transitions.

options.label: A guarded state transition with the current attempt/fencing token.
A lease timestamp alone, with no check at commit.
Whichever worker writes last should win.

questions.prompt: A webhook names a real job but its authenticity is unverified. What should happen before charging?
questions.explanation: A job ID identifies a resource; it does not authenticate the sender or prove completion. Verify the documented delivery authentication or fetch authoritative status. Logging after charging cannot prevent a forged side effect.

options.label: Trust the job ID as a secret signature.
Charge immediately, then log the sender address.
Verify supported authentication or reconcile through an authenticated status read.

questions.prompt: After a deploy, p95 preview latency rises while inference duration is flat. What should you inspect first?
questions.explanation: End-to-end latency includes stages outside inference. Compare deployment cohorts and traces to locate the increase. More GPU capacity may not help, and successful HTTP delivery does not prove a timely usable preview.

options.label: Ignore the problem because every HTTP request returns 200.
Per-stage traces and cohort changes across queueing, transfer, decode, and render.
Buy GPUs before measuring any other stage.

questions.prompt: The provider ignores AbortSignal and resolves after dispose. What prevents a stale render?
questions.explanation: Cancellation is a request to cooperating operations. A guard still prevents late local callbacks when cancellation is ignored; changing loading state cannot cancel an operation or prove remote work stopped.

options.label: AbortController guarantees the provider cannot return.
Removing the spinner cancels remote computation.
A disposed/revision guard before every UI callback.

questions.prompt: A fails after B was submitted. What should the coordinator do?
questions.explanation: Errors need the same revision guard as results: A no longer describes current intent. The slot must be released in finally so B can run; otherwise one old failure blocks all future work.

options.label: Keep the active slot occupied permanently.
Suppress A’s obsolete error and continue with B.
Show A’s error as if B failed.

questions.prompt: The active adapter never settles. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: Finally runs when control leaves the awaited operation, not after an implicit timeout. Promise.race changes which promise you await; it does not stop the remote operation. Define deadline, cancellation, and capacity policy explicitly.

options.label: The baseline blocks; a timeout alone does not prove remote work stopped.
The finally block runs after a fixed JavaScript timeout automatically.
Promise.race always cancels the losing operation.

questions.prompt: generate receives a mutable canvas object that is edited again before it reads the data. What is missing?
questions.explanation: A revision guard labels an operation but does not freeze its inputs. Snapshot the relevant state or use immutable revision references. A prompt-only cache omits identity, and component keys do not prevent object mutation.

options.label: A larger result cache keyed only by prompt.
A React component key to freeze the object.
An immutable input snapshot or stable revision reference.

questions.prompt: Can the same replace-newest-pending policy be used for accepted paid exports?
questions.explanation: Preview intents are replaceable by the agreed product contract. An accepted export is a durable commitment, so silently coalescing it loses work. A socket is a transport and does not survive failure as a job record.

options.label: Yes; a WebSocket connection is a durable queue.
No; accepted exports need durable identity and completion tracking.
Yes; older accepted exports can always be discarded.

exercises.title: Product Engineering 75-Minute Mock
exercises.briefing: This original, company-neutral rehearsal is not a reported interview question. Build a plain JavaScript preview coordinator, design durable paid exports, and defend two ownership stories. Use a local scratch file, blank diagram, and your own 75-minute timer. Assess your code and design yourself; the final checkpoint is scored. The mock interview article links to reference lessons. Attempt it first without AI tools or solutions.
objectives: Prove one active generation and one newest pending input with controlled promises.
Separate ephemeral previews from durable jobs, authorization, and charging.
Trace a provider-success/worker-crash scenario and a reconnect gap.
Explain an actual ownership decision with measurements and honest limits.

prediction.prompt: Before drawing the system, where do you expect the hardest correctness failure?

options.label: Stale previews overwrite the current intent.
A retry repeats an uncertain provider or billing effect.
Reconnect loses the authoritative job state.

steps.title: 0–5 minutes: clarify the contract
steps.instructions: An artist drags a slider faster than generation completes. Ask what may be coalesced, what must survive disconnect, what spends credits, and what current means. State that input is an immutable string snapshot and observers are synchronous/non-throwing. Separate observations from assumptions.

steps.title: 5–25 minutes: implement in plain JavaScript
steps.instructions: Write createPreviewCoordinator({generate, render, onError}) exposing submit(input) and dispose(). Keep at most one unsettled generation and one newest pending input. Suppress obsolete success/errors. generate(input, {signal}) may throw, reject, or ignore cancellation. dispose drops pending work and prevents later callbacks; submit after disposal throws. No frameworks or automatic retries.

steps.title: 25–30 minutes: prove the races
steps.instructions: Manually resolve A after B and C are submitted; only A then C may start and only C may render. Repeat with a stale rejection, a current rejection followed by recovery, a synchronous adapter throw, and disposal while A ignores abort. Explain O(1) bookkeeping/slots and why an adapter that never settles blocks the baseline.

steps.title: 30–45 minutes: make exports durable
steps.instructions: Assume 2,000 editors and two preview intents per second, private workspace assets, and success-only export charging with reservation. Draw acceptance, job state, atomic outbox, queue/worker, provider, asset, ledger, and status paths. Define tenant-scoped idempotency, immutable inputs, per-tenant admission, authorization, and reconnect snapshot/replay. Numbers and policies are exercise assumptions.

steps.title: 45–60 minutes: inject production failures
steps.instructions: The provider succeeds but the worker crashes before saving its result. Trace reconciliation and redelivery without duplicate capture; explain what happens if the provider lacks idempotency. Then drop a socket update, revoke access, and add 10× load. Finally p95 latency rises while inference stays flat: name the traces, containment, rollback evidence, and recovery checks you need.

steps.title: 60–70 minutes: defend two ownership stories
steps.instructions: Use the CRM migration and entitlement repair, or other real examples. Give each a 90-second version, then defend one rejected alternative and one failure mode. Verify the units and measurement window for any throughput claim. Separate your work, team contributions, source tests, artifact startup, deployment, and confirmed recovery.

steps.title: 70–75 minutes: score and ask
steps.instructions: Use the mock article’s six dimensions, each scored 0–4. Aim for 18/24 with none below 2 as a practice heuristic, not a hiring prediction. Pick one frontend/product question and one reliability/ownership question. Identify the weakest invariant and the next test that would improve it.

evidenceChecklist.label: I separated replaceable preview intents from durable accepted exports.
I demonstrated stale success, stale error, and disposal with controlled promises.
I proved a failed generation releases its slot and stated the never-settles limit.
I drew atomic job, reservation, and outbox acceptance.
I traced an unknown provider outcome without claiming exactly-once effects.
I explained versioned reconnect recovery and workspace authorization.
I defined user-facing signals and evidence needed to confirm recovery.
I rehearsed two factual ownership stories and scored all six rubric dimensions.

reflectionPrompts: Which invariant did your first implementation violate, and which test exposed it?
Where would your design still have an uncertain outcome or an unbounded resource?
What did you personally own in your story, and which measurement supports the result?
exercises.extensionChallenge: Repeat with two collaborators editing a five-node workflow while one is offline. Explain cycle detection, shared-document merge/undo, node-level durable attempts, downstream invalidation, and the boundary between CRDT convergence and authorized paid execution.

questions.prompt: A generic interview site lists likely company questions without candidate provenance. How should you use it?
questions.explanation: Likely questions are inferred practice material, not candidate evidence. Neither the exact loop nor a contradiction with a specific briefing follows. Confirm logistics directly and prioritize primary role and product material.

options.label: As optional speculation, not proof of the company’s actual questions.
As a verified question bank for the next interview.
As proof the supplied recruiter briefing is false.

questions.prompt: A product engineering role combines frontend and collaboration work with durable jobs. How should preparation change?
questions.explanation: The role spans product surfaces and reliability, so the interview preparation should connect them. Backend-only study misses explicit qualifications; syntax memorization alone cannot explain state ownership or user-visible correctness.

options.label: Memorize Svelte syntax instead of practicing invariants.
Include frontend state, rendering, product judgment, and collaboration boundaries.

questions.prompt: Your story says traffic grew from 500 to 50,000 RPM. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: Divide requests per minute by 60 and calculate the ratio as 50,000/500. Explain peak versus sustained, ingress versus processed events, and success rate so a capacity claim remains meaningful and defensible.

options.label: RPM is irrelevant if the architecture sounds scalable.
That is 100×, about 8.3 to 833 requests/second; define what was measured.

questions.prompt: Tests and a build pass after an incident fix. What can you honestly claim?
questions.explanation: Source validation does not establish the final pruned runtime, deployment state, or customer recovery. Separate each evidence layer and name unknown impact. Local dependencies can hide packaging failures.

options.label: Code validation passed; artifact startup, deployment, and recovery need their own evidence.
Customers are fully recovered with no data loss.
The production dependency graph must be correct because local tests passed.

questions.prompt: A founder says a new model and agent platform were showcased. What does that establish?
questions.explanation: A showcase supports knowledge of product direction. It does not establish availability, API guarantees, or the interview question. Ask how the announced work affects the role rather than converting a preview into a shipped contract.

options.label: Every customer can use a stable API for the new model now.
Your interview will definitely require agent framework coding.
A public showcase, not general availability or your interview format.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks why Pub/Sub instead of webhooks. What is the strongest response?
questions.explanation: A durable message system and HTTP push delivery address different layers and can be combined. Explain the actual requirements and failure ownership. Transport delivery guarantees do not automatically make arbitrary external side effects exactly once.

options.label: Pub/Sub guarantees all downstream effects happen exactly once.
Compare durability, replay, fan-out, and delivery ownership; Pub/Sub can also push over HTTP.
Webhooks cannot be used with any durable queue.

exercises.title: Cache Product Contract
exercises.prompt: Why is cache invalidation a product contract rather than only a cleanup task?
exercises.answer: It defines how stale the user experience may become, who owns truth, and what latency or recomputation cost the product accepts.
exercises.explanation: The article frames freshness as a product tradeoff. Different domains tolerate different stale states, so the cache strategy must match the user-facing contract.

exercises.title: Versioned Keys Cloze
exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the cache strategy that avoids deleting every derived key.
exercises.template: Use {{blank}} for composite views and computed projections where deleting every derived cache key is unreliable.
exercises.explanation: Versioned keys let new reads move to a fresh namespace while old derived keys expire naturally.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + です
languageGrammar.meaning: Make a polite statement identifying or describing something.
notes: Make a polite statement identifying or describing something.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + は
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the topic that the rest of the sentence comments on.
notes: Mark the topic that the rest of the sentence comments on.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + も
languageGrammar.meaning: Add that the same statement is true of another topic.
notes: Add that the same statement is true of another topic.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Sentence + か
languageGrammar.meaning: Turn a polite statement into a neutral question.
notes: Turn a polite statement into a neutral question.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + の + Noun
languageGrammar.meaning: Connect nouns for possession, affiliation, or description.
notes: Connect nouns for possession, affiliation, or description.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: これ・それ・あれ
languageGrammar.meaning: Point to a thing near the speaker, listener, or neither person.
notes: Point to a thing near the speaker, listener, or neither person.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: この・その・あの + Noun
languageGrammar.pattern: この・その・あの + Noun
languageGrammar.meaning: Point to a specific noun by its relative distance.
formation: この・その・あの + Noun
notes: Point to a specific noun by its relative distance.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: ここ・そこ・あそこ
languageGrammar.meaning: Point to locations near the speaker, listener, or farther away.
notes: Point to locations near the speaker, listener, or farther away.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: だれ・何・どこ・いつ
languageGrammar.pattern: だれ・何・どこ・いつ
languageGrammar.meaning: Ask for a person, thing, place, or time.
formation: だれ・何・どこ・いつ
notes: Ask for a person, thing, place, or time.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: あります・います
languageGrammar.meaning: State that an inanimate thing or animate being exists.
notes: State that an inanimate thing or animate being exists.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: There is a teacher in the classroom.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + が
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the grammatical subject, especially with existence and ability.
notes: Mark the grammatical subject, especially with existence and ability.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本があります。
examples.reading: 机の上に本があります。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: There is a book on the desk.

languageGrammar.title: Place + に
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark where something exists or the destination of movement.
notes: Mark where something exists or the destination of movement.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: There is a cat at home.

languageGrammar.title: Time + に
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark a specific time when an action occurs.
notes: Mark a specific time when an action occurs.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + から・まで
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the starting and ending point of time or place.
notes: Mark the starting and ending point of time or place.

examples.japanese: 九時から五時まで働きます。
examples.reading: 九時から五時まで働きます。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I work from nine to five.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + と + Noun
languageGrammar.meaning: Join nouns in a complete list meaning and.
notes: Join nouns in a complete list meaning and.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + や + Noun
languageGrammar.meaning: Give representative examples from a larger list.
notes: Give representative examples from a larger list.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
examples.reading: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: There are books, pens, and such on the desk.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ます
languageGrammar.meaning: Express a habitual or future action politely.
notes: Express a habitual or future action politely.

examples.japanese: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
examples.reading: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ません
languageGrammar.meaning: Express that a present or future action does not happen.
notes: Express that a present or future action does not happen.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ました
languageGrammar.meaning: Express a completed past action politely.
notes: Express a completed past action politely.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ませんでした
languageGrammar.pattern: Verb stem + ませんでした
languageGrammar.meaning: Express that an action did not happen in the past.
formation: Verb stem + ませんでした
notes: Express that an action did not happen in the past.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.reading: 朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + を + Verb
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the direct object affected by an action.
notes: Mark the direct object affected by an action.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Place + で + Verb
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the place where an action happens.
notes: Mark the place where an action happens.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Place + へ + movement verb
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the direction toward which someone moves.
notes: Mark the direction toward which someone moves.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Place + に + movement verb
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark a concrete destination or arrival point.
notes: Mark a concrete destination or arrival point.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Person + と
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the person who participates in an action with someone.
notes: Mark the person who participates in an action with someone.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Tool or vehicle + で
languageGrammar.meaning: Mark the means, instrument, language, or transport used.
notes: Mark the means, instrument, language, or transport used.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + をください
languageGrammar.meaning: Politely ask for an item in a shop or restaurant.
notes: Politely ask for an item in a shop or restaurant.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: て-form + ください
languageGrammar.meaning: Politely request that another person perform an action.
notes: Politely request that another person perform an action.

examples.japanese: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.reading: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: て-form + もいいです
languageGrammar.meaning: Ask for or grant permission to do something.
notes: Ask for or grant permission to do something.

examples.japanese: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: て-form + はいけません
languageGrammar.meaning: State that an action is prohibited.
notes: State that an action is prohibited.

examples.japanese: ここで食べてはいけません。
examples.reading: ここで食べてはいけません。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ましょう
languageGrammar.meaning: Invite someone to do an action together.
notes: Invite someone to do an action together.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + ませんか
languageGrammar.meaning: Invite someone politely while leaving room to decline.
notes: Invite someone politely while leaving room to decline.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: Would you like to watch a movie?

languageGrammar.title: Verb stem + たいです
languageGrammar.meaning: Express what the speaker wants to do.
notes: Express what the speaker wants to do.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I want to go to Japan.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + がほしいです
languageGrammar.meaning: Express that the speaker wants a thing.
notes: Express that the speaker wants a thing.

examples.japanese: 新しい自転車がほしいです。
examples.reading: 新しい自転車がほしいです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: い-adjective + Noun/です
languageGrammar.meaning: Describe a noun or make a polite statement with an i-adjective.
notes: Describe a noun or make a polite statement with an i-adjective.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: な-adjective + な + Noun
languageGrammar.meaning: Use a na-adjective before a noun or with です as a predicate.
notes: Use a na-adjective before a noun or with です as a predicate.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: くないです・ではありません
languageGrammar.pattern: くないです・ではありません
languageGrammar.meaning: Make i-adjectives and na-adjectives negative politely.
formation: くないです・ではありません
notes: Make i-adjectives and na-adjectives negative politely.

examples.japanese: この本は高くないです。
examples.reading: この本は高くないです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: かったです・でした
languageGrammar.meaning: Describe a past state with an adjective.
notes: Describe a past state with an adjective.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: A は B より adjective
languageGrammar.pattern: A は B より adjective
languageGrammar.meaning: Compare A with B using B as the reference point.
formation: A は B より adjective
notes: Compare A with B using B as the reference point.

examples.japanese: 電車はバスより速いです。
examples.reading: 電車はバスより速いです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: The train is faster than the bus.

languageGrammar.title: A より B のほうが adjective
languageGrammar.pattern: A より B のほうが adjective
languageGrammar.meaning: Say that B has more of a quality than A.
formation: A より B のほうが adjective
notes: Say that B has more of a quality than A.

examples.japanese: 肉より魚のほうが好きです。
examples.reading: 肉より魚のほうが好きです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I like fish more than meat.

languageGrammar.title: Group + で + Noun + が一番
languageGrammar.pattern: Group + で + Noun + が一番
languageGrammar.meaning: Identify the item with the greatest degree in a group.
formation: Group + で + Noun + が一番
notes: Identify the item with the greatest degree in a group.

examples.japanese: 果物でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.reading: 果物でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: Among fruits, I like apples best.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + が好き・嫌いです
languageGrammar.pattern: Noun + が好き・嫌いです
languageGrammar.meaning: Express likes and dislikes toward a noun or activity.
formation: Noun + が好き・嫌いです
notes: Express likes and dislikes toward a noun or activity.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + が上手・下手です
languageGrammar.pattern: Noun + が上手・下手です
languageGrammar.meaning: Describe skill or lack of skill in an activity.
formation: Noun + が上手・下手です
notes: Describe skill or lack of skill in an activity.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: My younger sister is good at cooking.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + が分かります
languageGrammar.meaning: State that someone understands a language or fact.
notes: State that someone understands a language or fact.

examples.japanese: 少し日本語が分かります。
examples.reading: 少し日本語が分かります。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Reason + から
languageGrammar.meaning: Give a simple reason for the following statement or choice.
notes: Give a simple reason for the following statement or choice.

examples.japanese: 雨ですから、家にいます。
examples.reading: 雨ですから、家にいます。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: Because it is raining, I will stay home.

languageGrammar.title: Noun/Verb dictionary form + 前に
languageGrammar.meaning: Place one action before another action or time.
notes: Place one action before another action or time.

examples.japanese: 寝る前に本を読みます。
examples.reading: 寝る前に本を読みます。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I read a book before sleeping.

languageGrammar.title: Noun/Verb past form + 後で
languageGrammar.meaning: Place an action after another event.
notes: Place an action after another event.

examples.japanese: 仕事の後で買い物します。
examples.reading: 仕事の後で買い物します。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Plain form + 時
languageGrammar.meaning: Describe what happens at a particular time or situation.
notes: Describe what happens at a particular time or situation.

examples.japanese: 日本へ行く時、カメラを買いました。
examples.reading: 日本へ行く時、カメラを買いました。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: When I went to Japan, I bought a camera.

languageGrammar.title: もう + past/affirmative
languageGrammar.meaning: Say that an expected action has already happened.
notes: Say that an expected action has already happened.

examples.japanese: もう昼ご飯を食べました。
examples.reading: もう昼ご飯を食べました。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: まだ + negative
languageGrammar.meaning: Say that an expected action has not happened yet.
notes: Say that an expected action has not happened yet.

examples.japanese: 宿題はまだ終わっていません。
examples.reading: 宿題はまだ終わっていません。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: The homework is not finished yet.

languageGrammar.title: て-form + います
languageGrammar.meaning: Describe an action in progress or a continuing state.
notes: Describe an action in progress or a continuing state.

examples.japanese: 今、新聞を読んでいます。
examples.reading: 今、新聞を読んでいます。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I am reading the newspaper now.

languageGrammar.title: て-form + から
languageGrammar.meaning: State that one action happens after another is completed.
notes: State that one action happens after another is completed.

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってから食べます。
examples.reading: 手を洗ってから食べます。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: I eat after washing my hands.

languageGrammar.title: past plain + り、past plain + りします
languageGrammar.pattern: past plain + り、past plain + りします
languageGrammar.meaning: List representative activities without claiming a complete list.
formation: past plain + り、past plain + りします
notes: List representative activities without claiming a complete list.

examples.japanese: 日曜日は本を読んだり散歩したりします。
examples.reading: 日曜日は本を読んだり散歩したりします。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: On Sundays I read and take walks, among other things.

languageGrammar.title: past plain + ことがあります
languageGrammar.pattern: past plain + ことがあります
languageGrammar.meaning: Say that someone has experienced an action before.
formation: past plain + ことがあります
notes: Say that someone has experienced an action before.

examples.japanese: 京都へ行ったことがあります。
examples.reading: 京都へ行ったことがあります。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: negative stem + なくてもいいです
languageGrammar.pattern: negative stem + なくてもいいです
languageGrammar.meaning: Say that an action is not required.
formation: negative stem + なくてもいいです
notes: Say that an action is not required.

examples.japanese: 明日は来なくてもいいです。
examples.reading: 明日は来なくてもいいです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: You do not have to come tomorrow.

languageGrammar.title: plain past/negative + ほうがいいです
languageGrammar.pattern: plain past/negative + ほうがいいです
languageGrammar.meaning: Give gentle advice about a preferable action.
formation: plain past/negative + ほうがいいです
notes: Give gentle advice about a preferable action.

examples.japanese: 早く寝たほうがいいです。
examples.reading: 早く寝たほうがいいです。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: You should go to bed early.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + だけ
languageGrammar.meaning: Limit a statement to only the marked item or amount.
notes: Limit a statement to only the marked item or amount.

examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.

languageGrammar.title: Noun + でも
languageGrammar.meaning: Offer one representative option in a casual suggestion.
notes: Offer one representative option in a casual suggestion.

examples.japanese: お茶でも飲みませんか。
examples.reading: お茶でも飲みませんか。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: Would you like tea or something?

languageGrammar.title: Sentence + ね
languageGrammar.meaning: Invite agreement or acknowledge shared information.
notes: Invite agreement or acknowledge shared information.

examples.japanese: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.reading: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: The weather is nice, isn't it?

languageGrammar.title: Sentence + よ
languageGrammar.meaning: Present information the listener may not know.
notes: Present information the listener may not know.

examples.japanese: この電車は東京へ行きますよ。
examples.reading: この電車は東京へ行きますよ。
examples.romaji: See the Japanese reading in the lesson.
examples.translation: This train goes to Tokyo, you know.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Advanced Next.js 16 One-Minute Briefs
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: One-minute reviews of Next.js rendering, caching, invalidation, performance, migration, and production failures for experienced engineers.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Experienced Next.js App Router engineers using short scrolling sessions for advanced production review.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Boundary First
cards.prompt: Classify the boundary before changing the flag.
cards.explanation: A Next.js review starts by naming cached, request-time, and client-owned work. Flags are implementation details after the boundary is clear.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Freshness Is Product
cards.prompt: Fresh data is not always required, but stale state must be named.
cards.explanation: A cache is safe only when the product accepts the stale state or the mutation path invalidates it quickly enough.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Trace The Read
cards.prompt: When data is stale, find the read function before changing route config.
cards.explanation: Adding broad no-store behavior can hide the actual stale cache key or missing tag. Trace route, component, read, tag, and mutation.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Narrow Suspense
cards.prompt: Wrap the slow runtime subtree, not the whole page.
cards.explanation: A narrow Suspense boundary preserves the useful shell and makes loading behavior clear.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Explicit Cache Snippet
cards.prompt: Use cache close to reusable work.
cards.explanation: Function-level caching keeps reuse policy near the data access and away from unrelated request-time UI.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Runtime Snippet
cards.prompt: Request-specific work should stay outside cached scopes.
cards.explanation: Runtime APIs such as cookies, headers, or connection-bound work describe the current request and should not silently affect shared cache output.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Explain The Boundary
cards.prompt: How would you explain cached versus request-time work to a team migrating to Next.js 16?
cards.explanation: With Cache Components, pages are dynamic by default; reusable work opts into cache, and Suspense protects the shell while runtime work resolves.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Debug Stale Data
cards.prompt: A user saves a record and still sees the old value. What do you inspect first?
cards.explanation: Inspect the read function, cache tags, mutation invalidation, and whether the UX requires updateTag rather than stale-while-revalidate.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Key Dimensions
cards.prompt: Tenant, locale, permissions, and variants are cache key dimensions.
cards.explanation: If output changes with a dimension, the cached scope must include it or avoid sharing that output.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Migration Packet
cards.prompt: Every migration PR should explain route behavior before and after.
cards.explanation: For Next.js 16, behavior review matters as much as codemod output because caching and request APIs affect user-visible correctness.

cards.title: Rendering Model: Tag Invalidation Snippet
cards.prompt: Tags should match the reads a mutation makes stale.
cards.explanation: Precise tags avoid both stale pages and global invalidation storms.

cards.title: Rendering Model: force-dynamic Review
cards.prompt: When should you keep force-dynamic in a Next.js 16 codebase?
cards.explanation: In Cache Components apps, usually you remove it. If the app still uses the previous model, keeping it requires a documented route-wide request-time and no-store contract.
