passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Langfuse And LangChain Flashcard Feed
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Passive AI engineering cards for reviewing LLM application architecture, LangChain, LangGraph, Langfuse tracing, RAG quality, evaluations, and risk governance.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Engineers learning to build, operate, evaluate, and govern production LLM applications.

cards.title: AI Product Loop
cards.prompt: A production LLM feature is a loop: build, trace, evaluate, and improve.
cards.explanation: The model call is only one part of the system. The product becomes reliable when prompt versions, retrieval, tools, traces, datasets, scores, and release decisions reinforce each other.

cards.title: Model As Dependency
cards.prompt: Treat the model as a probabilistic dependency, not as product logic by itself.
cards.explanation: The application still owns timeouts, retries, validation, output policy, fallbacks, tracing, and user-visible behavior even when a model creates the text.

cards.title: Trust Levels
cards.prompt: Separate user-controlled, system-controlled, and model-generated data.
cards.explanation: Separating data by who controls it prevents treating model output or retrieved text as authority and clarifies validation and safety review.

cards.title: Trace Early
cards.prompt: Add tracing before the first serious prompt iteration, not after production confusion.
cards.explanation: Without traces, teams argue from anecdotes. With traces, they can inspect prompt versions, context, tool calls, token usage, latency, errors, and evaluation outcomes.

cards.title: Fallback Is Behavior
cards.prompt: Design the fallback path as a product behavior, not an exception nobody sees.
cards.explanation: A clear fallback protects users when retrieval fails, tool calls error, confidence is low, or policy cannot be satisfied. It should be traced and evaluated.

cards.title: Cost Needs Context
cards.prompt: Debug model spend by feature, prompt version, model, token count, and user job.
cards.explanation: Aggregate cost alone rarely explains what changed. Feature and prompt metadata show whether the cost came from longer context, verbose outputs, retries, or model choice.

cards.title: Request Summary Snippet
cards.prompt: A compact request summary can power review dashboards and incident notes.
cards.explanation: Keep summaries structured and safe. They should expose review facts without copying unnecessary prompt or user content into logs.
cards.code:
const totalTokens = event.inputTokens + event.outputTokens;
const usedRetrieval = event.retrievedSourceIds.length > 0;

cards.title: Status Label Snippet
cards.prompt: Turn status and token usage into an explicit review label.
cards.explanation: Small deterministic helpers make production review repeatable. They are easier to test than logic hidden in prompt text.

cards.title: Safe Metadata Snippet
cards.prompt: Record ids and counts before copying raw content into telemetry.
cards.explanation: Source ids, prompt version, route, status, and counts often answer debugging questions without storing sensitive source material.

cards.title: Explain The Loop
cards.prompt: How would you explain the LLM application improvement loop to a backend engineer?
cards.explanation: Define the user’s task, record traces, build datasets from real cases, score outputs, and use evidence to promote changes.

cards.title: Prototype To Production
cards.prompt: What changes when an LLM prototype becomes a production feature?
cards.explanation: Production adds ownership of validation, privacy, cost, latency, fallbacks, evaluation, trace access, prompt change control, and incident response.

cards.title: Trust Boundary Review
cards.prompt: Why should model-generated tool arguments be validated outside the model?
cards.explanation: The model can propose data, but the application owns permissions, schemas, idempotency, and safety checks before any deterministic action runs.

cards.title: Tool Contract
cards.prompt: A LangChain tool should be narrow, named clearly, and backed by an input schema.
cards.explanation: A useful tool is not just a function. It is an application boundary where model intent becomes validated deterministic work.

cards.title: Structured Output
cards.prompt: Use structured output when downstream code needs fields instead of prose.
cards.explanation: Structured output helps extraction, routing, and automation, but the application still validates whether the returned shape is acceptable for the next step.

cards.title: RAG Is Context
cards.prompt: RAG retrieves trusted context and asks the model to answer from it.
cards.explanation: The model should not be expected to know product-specific or current facts from training. Retrieval supplies source material at request time.

cards.title: Start Small
cards.prompt: Use a simple chain before an agent when the steps are already known.
cards.explanation: A deterministic flow is easier to debug, test, trace, and secure. Add agent flexibility only when product behavior needs dynamic choice.

cards.title: Tool Permission
cards.prompt: Do not let a model bypass authorization just because it selected a tool.
cards.explanation: Tool calls cross from language generation into application action. Authorization, validation, and rate limits must stay outside the prompt.

cards.title: RAG Fallback
cards.prompt: A missing source should produce a clear fallback, not a confident guess.
cards.explanation: A RAG system is safer when it admits missing context. The fallback should be traced so teams can improve retrieval or source coverage.

cards.title: Tool Schema Snippet
cards.prompt: Tool schemas make model-selected actions reviewable and testable.
cards.explanation: The schema documents what the tool accepts and gives the application a validation point before any side effect happens.

cards.title: Router Snippet
cards.prompt: Low-confidence model classifications should not drive tool execution.
cards.explanation: Confidence thresholds are product policy. Keep them visible in code so they can be tested and reviewed.
cards.code: if (confidence < 0.75) return { needsHumanApproval: true, reason: 'low confidence' };

cards.title: RAG Source Snippet
cards.prompt: Pass source ids through the flow so answers can be reviewed later.
cards.explanation: Source ids connect retrieval, prompt context, citations, and evaluation. Without them, bad answers are harder to diagnose.

cards.title: Chain Or Agent
cards.prompt: How do you decide whether to use a simple chain or an agent?
cards.explanation: Start with deterministic workflows for known steps. Use agents only when dynamic tool or step selection is necessary.

cards.title: Tool Review
cards.prompt: What makes a LangChain tool safe enough for production?
cards.explanation: Safe tools are narrow, schema-validated, authorized, rate-limited, least-privilege, traced, and explicit about side effects.

cards.title: RAG Explanation
cards.prompt: Explain RAG to someone who thinks the model should already know the answer.
cards.explanation: RAG gives the model current trusted context at request time. It is useful for private, changing, or source-bound knowledge.

cards.title: Trace Timeline
cards.prompt: A trace is one request or task timeline across the LLM application.
cards.explanation: The trace lets engineers inspect prompt assembly, retrieval, tools, generation, output checks, errors, latency, tokens, and status in one place.

cards.title: Generation Observation
cards.prompt: A generation records model-specific behavior inside a trace.
cards.explanation: Generation observations are where prompt, response, model name, token usage, latency, and model errors become debuggable.

cards.title: Session Grouping
cards.prompt: A session groups related traces across a multi-turn user journey.
cards.explanation: Sessions help teams review a conversation or workflow that spans several requests while keeping each trace focused on one request or task.

cards.title: Safe Trace Metadata
cards.prompt: Prefer stable ids, counts, and labels over raw sensitive content in metadata.
cards.explanation: Good metadata makes traces searchable while reducing privacy risk. It should be designed intentionally rather than copied from request bodies.

cards.title: Cost Debugging
cards.prompt: Cost spikes need prompt version, model, context size, retries, and feature labels.
cards.explanation: Token counts alone do not tell the story. Teams need trace metadata that explains which release or product behavior changed.

cards.title: Stable Trace Shape
cards.prompt: A stable trace shape makes incidents easier to compare across requests.
cards.explanation: When every request has the same core observations, engineers can quickly spot missing retrieval, slow tools, model errors, and fallback branches.

cards.title: Trace Id Snippet
cards.prompt: Trace ids connect user reports, logs, datasets, and incident notes.
cards.explanation: A stable trace identifier lets teams move from a support ticket to the exact model and tool behavior behind it.

cards.title: Observation Snippet
cards.prompt: Name observations after product operations, not implementation trivia.
cards.explanation: Names like retrieve-policy and draft-answer remain understandable during incidents. Names like callHelper2 do not.

cards.title: Generation Metadata Snippet
cards.prompt: A generation should capture model identity and safe usage facts.
cards.explanation: Generation metadata helps compare model behavior, token usage, and latency across prompt versions and releases.

cards.title: Trace Anatomy
cards.prompt: What observations would you expect in a traced support-answer request?
cards.explanation: Expect intent classification, source retrieval, an optional tool call, model generation, an output check, and final status.

cards.title: Tracing And Privacy
cards.prompt: How do you keep traces useful without turning them into a data leak?
cards.explanation: Capture stable ids, versions, source references, and outcome metadata. Redact or avoid secrets, credentials, unnecessary personal data, and raw private documents.

cards.title: Trace Versus Session
cards.prompt: When would you use a session instead of only a trace?
cards.explanation: Use sessions when a user journey spans multiple traces, such as a multi-turn conversation or task with several requests.

cards.title: Prompt Version
cards.prompt: A prompt version is a product behavior version, not just a text edit.
cards.explanation: Prompt changes can affect tone, policy compliance, latency, cost, refusal behavior, and citation quality, so they need review and evaluation.

cards.title: Dataset
cards.prompt: A dataset stores examples used to test prompt and model behavior.
cards.explanation: Datasets make experiments repeatable. They should include easy cases, edge cases, missing context, and examples from production failures.

cards.title: Scores
cards.prompt: Scores turn LLM outputs into reviewable quality signals.
cards.explanation: Scores can be boolean, categorical, numeric, or text. Use the simplest shape that supports the release decision.

cards.title: Keep A Baseline
cards.prompt: Run experiments against the current production behavior before declaring a prompt better.
cards.explanation: A new prompt is only better relative to a baseline and the scores the product actually cares about.

cards.title: Hard Cases Matter
cards.prompt: A dataset with only happy paths will approve fragile prompts.
cards.explanation: Include ambiguity, missing context, adversarial phrasing, policy limits, and known previous failures to catch realistic regressions.

cards.title: Human Review
cards.prompt: Use human annotations when correctness depends on policy or domain judgment.
cards.explanation: Automated judges are useful, but some quality dimensions need domain experts to build ground truth and calibrate later automation.

cards.title: Grounding Score Snippet
cards.prompt: A grounding score can start as deterministic citation checks.
cards.explanation: Simple code evaluators can catch obvious failures before more expensive model-based review is needed.

cards.title: Decision Rule Snippet
cards.prompt: Write the experiment decision rule before running the experiment.
cards.explanation: A predeclared rule reduces cherry-picking and helps stakeholders agree on what quality means.

cards.title: Dataset Item Snippet
cards.prompt: Dataset items should include expected behavior, not just input text.
cards.explanation: Expected behavior can be an answer, refusal, escalation, or required source. This makes evaluation match product intent.
cards.code: const item = { input, expected: { behavior: 'escalate', reason: 'missing source' } };

cards.title: Prompt Release
cards.prompt: How would you release a new production prompt safely?
cards.explanation: Use versioning, trace linkage, dataset experiments, scoring, staged rollout, monitoring, and rollback.

cards.title: Score Design
cards.prompt: Why might one overall quality score be insufficient?
cards.explanation: Different risks need separate signals, such as groundedness, helpfulness, policy compliance, escalation correctness, latency, and cost.

cards.title: Dataset Source
cards.prompt: Why add production failure traces to evaluation datasets?
cards.explanation: Production failures reveal realistic cases that synthetic happy paths often miss. They turn incidents into regression coverage.

cards.title: RAG Quality Is System Quality
cards.prompt: RAG quality combines retrieval, context, prompts, output policy, and evaluation.
cards.explanation: A model cannot answer from trusted context if retrieval returns the wrong, stale, unauthorized, or excessive source material.

cards.title: Stale Source
cards.prompt: A stale source used to be correct but no longer represents current truth.
cards.explanation: Stale documents are dangerous because they produce plausible answers. Source versioning and freshness filters make this failure visible.

cards.title: Permission Filter
cards.prompt: RAG retrieval must respect what the user is allowed to see.
cards.explanation: A relevant source is not valid if the user lacks permission. Permission filters belong before prompt construction.

cards.title: Trace Source IDs
cards.prompt: Record source ids and versions for every RAG answer.
cards.explanation: Source ids let the team inspect whether retrieval, prompt context, citation behavior, or model generation caused a bad answer.

cards.title: Missing Context
cards.prompt: A good RAG assistant can say it does not have enough source context.
cards.explanation: Fallbacks are safer than unsupported answers. Missing-context cases should be represented in evaluation datasets.

cards.title: Citation Check
cards.prompt: A citation should support the claim it is attached to.
cards.explanation: Citation presence is not enough. Teams should review whether the cited source actually backs the generated answer.

cards.title: Citation Status Snippet
cards.prompt: Start citation checking by validating cited ids against retrieved ids.
cards.explanation: This does not prove semantic support, but it catches missing and unknown citations quickly.
cards.code:
const retrievedIds = new Set(sources.map((s) => s.id));
const unknown = answer.citedSourceIds.filter((id) => !retrievedIds.has(id));

cards.title: Context Budget Snippet
cards.prompt: Context budgets prevent retrieval from flooding the prompt.
cards.explanation: Token budgeting forces the retriever and prompt builder to prioritize the strongest evidence instead of dumping everything into context.

cards.title: Fallback Snippet
cards.prompt: Use explicit fallback status when sources are insufficient.
cards.explanation: Explicit status makes missing-context cases searchable in traces and reusable as evaluation examples.

cards.title: RAG Failure Modes
cards.prompt: Name three RAG failure modes and how you would observe them.
cards.explanation: Strong answers include no hit, wrong hit, stale source, permission leak, context overload, and citation mismatch with trace fields for each.

cards.title: RAG Dataset
cards.prompt: What cases belong in a RAG evaluation dataset?
cards.explanation: Include factual lookup, ambiguity, missing answer, stale policy, permission boundaries, multi-document synthesis, and adversarial retrieved text.

cards.title: RAG With Langfuse
cards.prompt: How does Langfuse help debug bad RAG answers?
cards.explanation: Langfuse traces connect the question, retrieval query, source ids, prompt context, generation, citations, fallback status, and scores.

cards.title: Dynamic Choice
cards.prompt: Use an agent when the model needs to choose steps or tools.
cards.explanation: If the workflow is known, a deterministic graph or chain is easier to test and operate. Agent flexibility has real risk and cost.

cards.title: LangGraph Durability
cards.prompt: LangGraph is for durable execution, streaming, persistence, and human-in-the-loop control.
cards.explanation: Graph state and checkpoints matter when workflows need to pause, resume, stream progress, or survive beyond a single request.

cards.title: Human Approval
cards.prompt: Human approval is a design control for high-impact tool actions.
cards.explanation: Approval is appropriate for money movement, external messages, sensitive access, destructive actions, and legal or policy commitments.

cards.title: Least Privilege Tools
cards.prompt: Give agents narrow tools instead of one powerful general-purpose tool.
cards.explanation: Narrow tools are easier to authorize, validate, rate limit, trace, and review. Broad tools make model mistakes more dangerous.

cards.title: Idempotency Review
cards.prompt: Write-capable tools need idempotency and retry rules before production.
cards.explanation: Agents may retry or resume. Without idempotency, one user request can accidentally create duplicate side effects.

cards.title: Trace The Approval
cards.prompt: Trace both the model proposal and the human approval decision.
cards.explanation: Auditability requires the planned action, validated arguments, approving actor, decision time, and final tool result.

cards.title: Permission Matrix Snippet
cards.prompt: A permission matrix keeps agent tool authority visible in code.
cards.explanation: Visible permission logic is testable. Hidden permission logic inside a prompt is not enough for production side effects.

cards.title: Tool Budget Snippet
cards.prompt: Tool-call budgets protect systems from runaway agent loops.
cards.explanation: Budgets make stopping conditions explicit and help contain cost, latency, and dependency pressure.

cards.title: Approval Interrupt Snippet
cards.prompt: Durable workflows can pause for human approval before continuing.
cards.explanation: Human-in-the-loop interrupts are useful when a model proposes a high-impact action that needs explicit review.
cards.code: const approval = interrupt({ action: 'issue_refund', amount, invoiceId });

cards.title: Agent Operations
cards.prompt: What operational controls does a production agent need?
cards.explanation: Strong answers include tool schemas, least privilege, approval gates, budgets, tracing, checkpoint rules, idempotency, and fallback behavior.

cards.title: Why LangGraph
cards.prompt: When would you reach for LangGraph instead of a simple LangChain agent?
cards.explanation: Use LangGraph when you need explicit state, checkpoints, streaming, resume, interrupts, human-in-the-loop, or complex workflow control.

cards.title: Approval Design
cards.prompt: What should a human approval screen show before an agent writes data?
cards.explanation: Show the user request, proposed action, tool name, validated arguments, expected side effect, risk, and cancel or rollback options.

cards.title: Prompt Injection
cards.prompt: Prompt injection happens when user or external text steers model behavior unexpectedly.
cards.explanation: Prompt injection can be direct or indirect. Retrieved content should be treated as data, not as trusted instructions.

cards.title: Sensitive Data
cards.prompt: LLM traces, datasets, prompts, and outputs can all become data exposure surfaces.
cards.explanation: Decide what to store, redact, hash, exclude, and retain before production. Trace usefulness does not justify unnecessary sensitive data capture.

cards.title: Excessive Agency
cards.prompt: An agent has excessive agency when it can do more than the product task requires.
cards.explanation: Least privilege applies to conversational systems too. Do not give summarizers write tools or support bots unrestricted financial actions.

cards.title: Layered Controls
cards.prompt: Prompt wording alone does not solve LLM security risk.
cards.explanation: Use separation of instructions and data, validation, least privilege, approval gates, tracing, evaluation, and incident response together.

cards.title: Incident Packet
cards.prompt: LLM incidents need prompt version, model, trace ids, source ids, tool calls, and rollback path.
cards.explanation: These facts let teams reconstruct what happened and decide whether the issue came from prompt, retrieval, model, tool, or policy behavior.

cards.title: Govern Map Measure Manage
cards.prompt: Use AI risk frameworks as practical operating loops, not paperwork.
cards.explanation: Govern ownership, map risks, measure behavior, and manage mitigations across the feature lifecycle. This aligns policy with engineering practice.

cards.title: Risk Classifier Snippet
cards.prompt: Risk classifiers should fail closed for sensitive data and write actions.
cards.explanation: Simple deterministic gates can prevent the model from turning uncertain or high-risk requests into immediate side effects.

cards.title: Injection Flag Snippet
cards.prompt: Flag external instructions found in retrieved content for review.
cards.explanation: External instructions are not automatically malicious, but they should not be allowed to override system instructions or tool policy.

cards.title: Retention Snippet
cards.prompt: Trace retention should be explicit and matched to incident needs.
cards.explanation: Retention policy balances debugging value, privacy risk, compliance expectations, and cost.

cards.title: Prompt Injection Review
cards.prompt: How do you mitigate prompt injection in a RAG application?
cards.explanation: Strong answers separate instructions from data, validate tool calls, limit authority, trace behavior, include adversarial evals, and fail closed when uncertain.

cards.title: AI Governance
cards.prompt: What does practical AI governance look like for an engineering team?
cards.explanation: It includes owners, source-of-truth prompts, change logs, eval datasets, trace controls, incident playbooks, risk reviews, and release gates.

cards.title: Trace Data Risk
cards.prompt: What data protection questions should be answered before enabling LLM tracing?
cards.explanation: Ask what is captured, who can access it, how it is redacted, how long it is retained, and whether datasets copy production content.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: BFS And DFS Scrolling Review
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Short traversal concepts, implementation reminders, code snippets, and interview prompts for mobile review.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Developers learning graph traversal or preparing BFS and DFS coding interview patterns.

cards.title: BFS Uses A Queue
cards.prompt: Breadth-first search expands nodes in first-in, first-out discovery order.
cards.explanation: The queue preserves distance layers, so every node d edges away is expanded before any node d plus one edges away.

cards.title: DFS Uses A Stack
cards.prompt: Depth-first search follows one branch before it backtracks.
cards.explanation: Recursion uses the runtime call stack; iterative DFS makes the same pending path explicit with a stack collection.

cards.title: Visited Prevents Cycles
cards.prompt: A general graph traversal needs a record of nodes already discovered.
cards.explanation: Without visited state, a cycle can repeat forever and shared neighbors can be processed many times.

cards.title: Shortest Often Means BFS
cards.prompt: Equal-cost moves plus a minimum-step question are the classic BFS signal.
cards.explanation: BFS explores increasing path lengths. The first target discovery is optimal when every edge has the same cost.

cards.title: Weights Change The Algorithm
cards.prompt: Plain BFS does not solve shortest paths with different edge costs.
cards.explanation: The layer number counts edges, not total weight. Nonnegative weighted paths usually call for Dijkstra's algorithm.

cards.title: Mark Before Enqueue
cards.prompt: Mark a BFS neighbor visited at the moment it enters the queue.
cards.explanation: Early marking prevents two parents in the same frontier from enqueueing the same shared neighbor.

cards.title: TypeScript Queue Head
cards.prompt: Advance a head index instead of repeatedly shifting an array-backed queue.
cards.explanation: The array keeps queued values while head identifies the next item, avoiding repeated front removal and reindexing.

cards.title: Python Queue Pop
cards.prompt: Python deque provides efficient removal from the front of the BFS queue.
cards.explanation: Use popleft for FIFO order; list pop without an index removes from the end and behaves like a stack.
cards.code:
from collections import deque
queue = deque([start])
node = queue.popleft()

cards.title: Depth Can Break Recursion
cards.prompt: Use iterative DFS when graph depth is large or controlled by untrusted input.
cards.explanation: An explicit stack preserves DFS behavior without depending on the runtime's limited recursive call stack.

cards.title: Grid Becomes A Graph
cards.prompt: In Number Of Islands, what are the vertices, edges, and connected components?
cards.explanation: Land cells are vertices, orthogonal land adjacencies are edges, and each maximal connected component is one island.

cards.title: Two Correct Island Traversals
cards.prompt: BFS and DFS both count islands in O(rows times cols) time.
cards.explanation: The prompt needs complete component discovery, so internal traversal order does not change the count; memory shape and recursion safety differ.

cards.title: DFS Finds Back Edges
cards.prompt: A prerequisite edge to a node on the active DFS path proves a directed cycle.
cards.explanation: The visiting color means that dependency has not finished; reaching it again closes a cycle in the active chain.

cards.title: Kahn Starts At Zero
cards.prompt: BFS topological processing begins with every course whose indegree is zero.
cards.explanation: Removing ready courses can make dependents ready. A cycle leaves some courses with positive indegree forever.

cards.title: Both Are Linear
cards.prompt: Adjacency-list BFS and DFS both take O(V + E) time with visited tracking.
cards.explanation: Every reachable vertex is processed once, and every adjacency-list edge is inspected a constant number of times.

cards.title: Shape Drives Memory
cards.prompt: BFS stores a frontier; DFS stores an active path and pending branches.
cards.explanation: A FIFO frontier is wide on broad graphs; recursive DFS is deep on long paths. The lesson’s TS queue retains processed entries (O(V)); its iterative DFS marks on pop and may retain duplicate pending entries (O(E)). Do not infer memory solely from the algorithm name.

cards.title: Explain Before Coding
cards.prompt: State the node, edge, visited rule, and traversal invariant before implementation.
cards.explanation: A precise model turns a story problem into a standard traversal and gives the interviewer a clear correctness argument.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Database Indexes And Search Flashcard Feed
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Passive database index, PostgreSQL search, and connection pooling cards for short mobile review sessions.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Backend, full-stack, and platform engineers reviewing database indexing, search, and connection management.

cards.title: Indexes Are Read Models
cards.prompt: A database index is a maintained read structure with ongoing costs.
cards.explanation: Every index trades faster matching query shapes for write overhead, storage, vacuum work, and migration cost. Review the workload that pays for it.

cards.title: Leftmost Prefix
cards.prompt: Composite B-tree indexes are strongest when queries constrain leading columns in order.
cards.explanation: An index on account_id and created_at is designed around account first. A query that only filters created_at may not benefit much.

cards.title: GIN Is Inverted
cards.prompt: GIN stores component keys such as lexemes, trigrams, or array elements.
cards.explanation: Instead of one scalar key per row, GIN maps extracted components to candidate rows. That makes it fit containment and text search shapes.

cards.title: Document Meets Query
cards.prompt: PostgreSQL full text search matches tsquery against tsvector with @@.
cards.explanation: The document and query are both parsed into normalized search structures before matching; this is not raw substring search.

cards.title: Rank Is Local
cards.prompt: ts_rank and ts_rank_cd are ordering signals inside one query, not universal relevance percentages.
cards.explanation: Normalization can scale scores, but it does not make ranks comparable across unrelated queries or a durable product quality metric.

cards.title: Trigrams Handle Typos
cards.prompt: pg_trgm compares overlapping three-character fragments to find similar strings.
cards.explanation: A misspelling can still share enough trigrams with the intended word for useful candidate generation.

cards.title: Threshold Is Tuning
cards.prompt: pg_trgm.similarity_threshold decides which fuzzy candidates the % operator admits.
cards.explanation: Lower thresholds help typo-heavy short searches but increase candidate volume and irrelevant matches. Tune with real search examples.

cards.title: Hybrid Candidate Sets
cards.prompt: Hybrid search often combines precise FTS candidates with fuzzy trigram candidates.
cards.explanation: FTS catches exact lexeme matches. Trigrams catch typos. The ranking layer decides how those signals compete.

cards.title: Index Review
cards.prompt: Before adding an index, name the exact query shape it supports.
cards.explanation: If the index cannot be tied to a real predicate, sort, and result size, it is likely to become maintenance cost without clear benefit.

cards.title: Partial Index Fit
cards.prompt: Use partial indexes for stable hot subsets, not as a substitute for partitioning.
cards.explanation: The query predicate must imply the index predicate. Many overlapping partial indexes can make planning and maintenance worse.

cards.title: Expression Must Match
cards.prompt: An expression index on lower(name) expects queries to use lower(name).
cards.explanation: Changing the query to raw name or unaccent(lower(name)) changes the indexed expression and may prevent index usage.

cards.title: Choose Search Config
cards.prompt: Use simple or english text search configuration intentionally.
cards.explanation: English stemming helps prose. Simple configuration can be better for titles, names, tags, codes, and labels where literal matching matters.

cards.title: Store The Vector
cards.prompt: Frequently searched documents usually deserve a stored tsvector or generated column.
cards.explanation: Recomputing to_tsvector in every query can be wasteful. Stored vectors make the query and matching GIN index easier to reason about.

cards.title: Use SET LOCAL
cards.prompt: Use SET LOCAL for request-specific trigram thresholds on pooled connections.
cards.explanation: A plain SET can leak a relaxed threshold into later requests on the same connection. SET LOCAL clears when the transaction ends.

cards.title: Extensions Are Setup
cards.prompt: CREATE EXTENSION belongs in migrations or database setup, not every search query.
cards.explanation: Extensions create database objects. Search requests should assume the schema exists and only tune request-local settings when needed.

cards.title: Tie-Break Search Results
cards.prompt: Add a deterministic tie-breaker after rank, such as id.
cards.explanation: Stable ordering matters for repeatable tests and pagination. Rank alone can leave equal-score rows in unstable order.

cards.title: Compound B-Tree Snippet
cards.prompt: Read the index order as account first, recent orders second.
cards.explanation: The query must use account_id for this index to be highly selective before created_at ordering matters.
cards.code:
create index orders_account_created_idx
  on orders (account_id, created_at desc);

cards.title: Partial Index Snippet
cards.prompt: Read the predicate as part of the index contract.
cards.explanation: Only unfulfilled orders are indexed. Queries must include or imply fulfilled_at is null to use this index.

cards.title: Weighted Vector Snippet
cards.prompt: Read title as A weight and body as C weight.
cards.explanation: setweight lets title matches outrank body-only matches when ranking consults the weighted vector.

cards.title: FTS GIN Snippet
cards.prompt: Read this as a GIN index over a stored search document.
cards.explanation: The search query should use the same search_document column with @@ so the index can filter candidates.

cards.title: Drizzle Trigram Snippet
cards.prompt: Read this as a GIN trigram expression index over lower(name).
cards.explanation: gin_trgm_ops tells PostgreSQL to extract trigram keys from the lower(name) expression for fuzzy matching.

cards.title: Trigram Query Snippet
cards.prompt: Read % as candidate admission and similarity as ranking.
cards.explanation: The WHERE clause can use the trigram index, while ORDER BY ranks the filtered candidate set.
cards.code:
where lower(title) % lower($1)
order by similarity(lower(title), lower($1)) desc

cards.title: Hybrid Candidates Snippet
cards.prompt: Read UNION ALL as keeping both FTS and trigram evidence.
cards.explanation: Rows can come from both passes. A later grouped score can keep the best signal or add a combined-match bonus.
cards.code:
select id, fts_rank as rank from fts_candidates
union all
select id, trigram_rank as rank from trigram_candidates

cards.title: SET LOCAL Snippet
cards.prompt: Read this as request-scoped threshold tuning.
cards.explanation: The threshold applies within the transaction and clears when the transaction ends.

cards.title: Index Cost Interview
cards.prompt: A teammate says every frequently filtered column should get an index. How do you respond?
cards.explanation: A strong answer discusses exact query shape, selectivity, returned rows, write amplification, storage, migration risk, and plan verification.

cards.title: Partial Index Interview
cards.prompt: When would you use a partial index instead of a normal index?
cards.explanation: Use it when a stable predicate selects a small hot subset and the target queries include or imply that predicate.

cards.title: FTS Versus LIKE Interview
cards.prompt: Why is full text search different from lower(body) like '%term%'?
cards.explanation: FTS parses documents into lexemes and queries into tsquery values. LIKE is character pattern matching and has different index behavior.

cards.title: Rank Caveat Interview
cards.prompt: Why should a product not display ts_rank_cd as a percent match?
cards.explanation: The score is a query-local ranking signal and does not use global corpus statistics. It is useful for ordering, not universal quality.

cards.title: Trigram Index Interview
cards.prompt: Explain what lower(name) gin_trgm_ops means in a PostgreSQL index.
cards.explanation: It is a trigram operator-class index over the lower(name) expression. Compatible queries must use the same normalized expression.

cards.title: Threshold Tuning Interview
cards.prompt: What can go wrong when pg_trgm.similarity_threshold is lowered too far?
cards.explanation: More weak matches enter the candidate set, increasing ranking work, latency, and irrelevant results unless other filters and ranking signals control it.

cards.title: Hybrid Ranking Interview
cards.prompt: Why might a hybrid query multiply trigram similarity by 0.8?
cards.explanation: It is a business weighting choice that lets exact FTS matches usually outrank fuzzy typo matches with similar raw scores.

cards.title: Extension Placement Interview
cards.prompt: Why should CREATE EXTENSION not live in a normal search query?
cards.explanation: Extensions are schema setup. Runtime search should rely on migrated database capabilities and keep request-specific settings transaction-local.

cards.title: HOT Needs Two Conditions
cards.prompt: A HOT update changes no regular-index dependency and keeps the new tuple on the original heap page.
cards.explanation: Both the logical index rule and the physical page-space rule must hold. HOT is decided for each updated row, not enabled once for an entire table.

cards.title: One Index Entry, Many Versions
cards.prompt: A HOT chain lets one index entry reach successive same-page row versions.
cards.explanation: The root page item leads through tuple links to the visible version. Page pruning can later remove intermediate versions no snapshot needs.

cards.title: Audit Hidden Index Dependencies
cards.prompt: Check keys, INCLUDE payloads, expressions, and partial predicates before calling a column unindexed.
cards.explanation: Updating any of those regular-index dependencies blocks HOT. On PostgreSQL 16+, BRIN is the summarizing-index exception, though its summary may still change.

cards.title: Measure Before Lowering Fillfactor
cards.prompt: Reserve page space for proven update pressure, not to maximize a context-free HOT percentage.
cards.explanation: Lower fillfactor can improve same-page update capacity, but the larger heap can cost scans, cache density, and storage. Changing it does not repack existing pages.

cards.title: HOT-Eligible Update Snippet
cards.prompt: This update can be HOT when last_seen_at is unindexed and the original page has room.
cards.explanation: The primary-key index finds the row but is not modified. Eligibility disappears if another regular index references last_seen_at.

cards.title: HOT Monitoring Snippet
cards.prompt: Compare HOT updates with all updates over a known interval.
cards.explanation: The guarded division avoids dividing by zero. Statistics are cumulative and can reset, so an interval trend is more useful than one lifetime ratio.

cards.title: HOT Versus Read Index Interview
cards.prompt: A new index on a frequently updated timestamp drops the HOT ratio. Should you remove it?
cards.explanation: Measure the read path the index supports against update amplification, WAL, bloat, and maintenance. Neither a read index nor a HOT ratio wins without workload evidence.

cards.title: HOT Does Not Replace Vacuum
cards.prompt: Why does a table with mostly HOT updates still need autovacuum?
cards.explanation: Vacuum still reclaims other dead versions and index entries, maintains visibility information, supports planner statistics, and prevents transaction-ID wraparound.

cards.title: Clients Are Not Backends
cards.prompt: A transaction pooler separates client socket lifetime from backend transaction lifetime.
cards.explanation: After a transaction finishes and cleanup completes, another client can use that backend. Simultaneous demand beyond backend capacity must wait or fail admission.

cards.title: Hold Time Sets Occupancy
cards.prompt: At 600 transactions/s and 0.04 s mean backend hold time, average occupancy is 24.
cards.explanation: This mean relationship is not a p99 sizing rule. Holding transactions open during remote calls consumes backends even without active SQL.

cards.title: Count Every Pool
cards.prompt: Budget peak pods × processes × pools × per-pool max, then add other consumers.
cards.explanation: Include old/new overlap, jobs, and direct tools. A singleton per process still multiplies across the fleet. A pool aimed at a different server belongs in that server budget.

cards.title: Drain Before Closing Pools
cards.prompt: Stop admission and job intake, drain bounded work, then await pool closure before exiting.
cards.explanation: A preStop hook consumes Kubernetes grace time. Provider interruption warnings may be best effort. Cleanup cannot guarantee immediate backend release after node loss.

cards.title: Headroom Is Part Of The Limit
cards.prompt: Calculate the per-pool ceiling using the same-server budget.
cards.explanation: The example leaves 187 slots for reserves/headroom and 200 for other consumers. It assumes those reserves were not already deducted from 1,187. The result is illustrative, not a Titan setting.

cards.title: Pooler Replicas Multiply Too
cards.prompt: Three replicas with two 80-backend pools each, plus 120 direct connections, permit 600.
cards.explanation: A fourth overlapping replica raises the ceiling to 760. Client admission limits are separate from database backend limits.

cards.title: Would You Change Only The URL?
cards.prompt: A staging SELECT passes through a pooler. Is the application ready for transaction mode?
cards.explanation: No. Validate the pinned pooler and driver, tenant/session state, prepared statement protocols, listeners, rollback, cancellation, and reconnect behavior using fixtures.

cards.title: A Lost COMMIT Response
cards.prompt: A connection drops after a write sends COMMIT. Should the application retry immediately?
cards.explanation: The result is uncertain. Reconcile through durable operation identity or a proven idempotent design; use bounded retries. Neither success nor rollback is established by a missing response.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Frontend Interview Review
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Forty-two cards review the requirements, approaches, pitfalls, and language-specific details of the seven frontend interview challenges.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Engineers reinforcing interview reasoning after guided practice.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Contract
cards.prompt: Which small input best exposes an accidental square-board assumption?
cards.explanation: 2 rows and 3 columns. A non-square board requires independent bounds. Square and single-cell cases can pass even when the column loop incorrectly uses the row count.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Reasoning
cards.prompt: With 3 columns, what are the coordinates of flat index 5?
cards.explanation: Row 1, column 2. Integer division 5 // 3 gives row 1 and remainder 5 % 3 gives column 2. Dividing by the row count swaps the contract and fails rectangular inputs.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Pitfall
cards.prompt: Python: rows = [[0] * 3] * 2; rows[0][0] = 9. What happens?
cards.explanation: Both rows begin with 9. List multiplication repeats references to the same inner list. Allocate each inner list in a comprehension to preserve row independence; nested assignment itself is legal.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Clarify independent dimensions → Create a small rectangular model → Render the coordinates → Test resizing and explain identity. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Each iteration allocates a fresh row, so changing row zero does not change row one.

cards.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Each iteration allocates a fresh row, so changing row zero does not change row one.

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Contract
cards.prompt: Which requirement guarantees exactly 10 zeros?
cards.explanation: Sample 10 distinct positions without replacement. Independent per-cell probability gives an expected count, not an exact count. Independent position draws can collide, so overwriting may produce fewer than 10 zeros.

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Reasoning
cards.prompt: Why is sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) unsuitable for a uniform shuffle?
cards.explanation: A random comparator violates sorting’s ordering assumptions, so it cannot establish uniform permutation probabilities and yields implementation-dependent bias. Fisher–Yates has a direct uniformity argument under uniform independent draws.

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Pitfall
cards.prompt: Partial shuffle: at iteration i, where must j be sampled?
cards.explanation: From i through n - 1, inclusive. The prefix before i is already fixed. Sampling the remaining suffix preserves uniqueness and gives each remaining position an equal chance to enter the selected prefix.

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Clarify exact k and bounds → Sample unique flat indexes → Project fresh matrix rows → Store output and test regeneration. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Partial Fisher–Yates fixes one new selected position using the remaining suffix. The pool and output still require linear storage.
cards.code:
const j = i + Math.floor(random() * (n - i));
[pool[i], pool[j]] = [pool[j], pool[i]];

cards.title: Randomized Zero Matrix: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Partial Fisher–Yates fixes one new selected position using the remaining suffix. The pool and output still require linear storage.
cards.code:
j = i + int(rng() * (n - i))
pool[i], pool[j] = pool[j], pool[i]

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Contract
cards.prompt: Where does a click at row 1, column 2 place a token?
cards.explanation: In that exact empty cell. This 5×5 brief is click-to-place. Gravity belongs to the separate 6×7 challenge. A familiar game rule must not silently replace the actual requirement.

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Reasoning
cards.prompt: What happens after a click on an occupied cell?
cards.explanation: The board and current player stay unchanged. A rejected move does not consume a turn. Returning the existing state preserves both ownership and board contents, making this invariant simple to test.

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Pitfall
cards.prompt: Do four matching diagonal tokens win under the stated contract?
cards.explanation: No; the source specifies only horizontal and vertical runs. Diagonal detection is a useful extension only after agreement; board fullness does not change the allowed directions.

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Render the 5×5 board → Reject invalid moves → Place a token and check the result → Advance only a valid nonterminal turn. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: A terminal guard belongs in the transition as well as the UI. It prevents queued or programmatic moves from changing a finished game.

cards.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: A terminal guard belongs in the transition as well as the UI. It prevents queued or programmatic moves from changing a finished game.
cards.code:
if game["winner"] or game["draw"]:
    return game

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Contract
cards.prompt: A user clicks the top cell in column 2. Where does the token go?
cards.explanation: Into the lowest empty cell in column 2. Clicking identifies a column; the illustrated rule applies gravity within that column. The chosen row is determined by occupancy, not by pointer height.

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Reasoning
cards.prompt: What happens when the selected column is full?
cards.explanation: Reject the move and preserve the current player. A full column has no legal insertion point. Changing columns or overwriting silently changes the move, while changing the player would consume a rejected turn.

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Pitfall
cards.prompt: How must directional counting treat the newly placed token?
cards.explanation: Count it once, then scan outward in both directions. Starting at one and adding matching neighbors avoids double-counting the center. Counting it in both directions can incorrectly declare a three-token run a win.

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Identify the clicked column → Find its lowest empty cell → Place and check horizontal/vertical wins → Preserve terminal state or advance the turn. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Scan upward from the bottom. If row becomes negative, the column is full and the current player must keep their turn.
cards.code:
row = ROWS - 1;
while (row >= 0 && board[row][column] !== null) row--;

cards.title: Column-drop 6×7 Game: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Scan upward from the bottom. If row becomes negative, the column is full and the current player must keep their turn.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Contract
cards.prompt: How should an empty folder be identified?
cards.explanation: By its explicit type, even when children is empty. Files can have extensionless names and folders can be empty. The discriminated type is the structural contract, so child count and name heuristics are unreliable.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Reasoning
cards.prompt: Why are filenames unsuitable as the general key?
cards.explanation: Different nodes can have the same filename. Stable unique IDs preserve identity even when names repeat or change. React accepts string keys; generating new keys on each toggle would reset component state.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Pitfall
cards.prompt: What happens to local child state when its conditional subtree unmounts?
cards.explanation: It resets when the child is mounted again. Removing the child from the rendered tree destroys its local state. A parent-owned expanded-ID set can retain the preference independently of child mounting.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Define file and folder types → Handle the empty root list → Render FileItem recursively → Test collapse ownership and hierarchy lines. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Copy expansion state before removal. A parent-owned set retains hidden descendant IDs, so reopening can preserve their expansion.

cards.title: Recursive File Explorer: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Copy expansion state before removal. A parent-owned set retains hidden descendant IDs, so reopening can preserve their expansion.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Contract
cards.prompt: Filtering for "SCRIPT" should match which option?
cards.explanation: TypeScript. The contract is a case-insensitive substring match anywhere in the label. Normalize the query and label consistently before checking inclusion.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Reasoning
cards.prompt: What should a matching disabled option do?
cards.explanation: Stay visible and reject selection. Unavailable choices are explicitly visible in the brief. Enforce disabled status in both the control and the state transition so alternate interaction paths cannot select them.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Pitfall
cards.prompt: What changes atomically when an enabled option is selected?
cards.explanation: Add its ID, clear the query, and derive a list without that ID. Selection adds rather than replaces. Deriving the list from current IDs and query avoids synchronization bugs, while clearing the query satisfies the explicit interaction contract.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Define IDs and selection state → Derive matching unselected options → Apply guarded selection and removal → Test keyboard and outside dismissal. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Derive the list from options, selected IDs, and query. Do not filter disabled choices out; reject their selection separately.

cards.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Derive the list from options, selected IDs, and query. Do not filter disabled choices out; reject their selection separately.
cards.code:
[o for o in options if o["id"] not in selected
 and query.lower() in o["label"].lower()]

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Contract
cards.prompt: What is the corrected repository endpoint for username ada?
cards.explanation: /users/ada/repos. GitHub lists a user’s repositories under /users/{username}/repos. The supplied brief has a malformed URL, which should be clarified rather than copied into working code.

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Reasoning
cards.prompt: A first page has 100 repositories and a second has 3. What is the count?
cards.explanation: 103. Counting only the first response undercounts paginated results. Sum all pages until the listing ends; the fixture is stable so the expected total is exactly 103.

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Pitfall
cards.prompt: When should cells be assigned to users?
cards.explanation: Once after loading the user list, before individual counts arrive. Assignments are part of this load’s state. Preassigning them prevents response order and unrelated renders from moving users or causing collisions.

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Recipe
cards.prompt: How would you start the baseline under interview time pressure?
cards.explanation: Load and validate usernames → Assign unique cells → Fetch every user page with lifecycle guards → Publish counts and per-user errors. Explain one invariant and one adverse case before optimizing.

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Typescript
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Check again after awaiting work. An adapter can ignore cancellation, so a pre-request check alone cannot prevent late local publication.
cards.code:
const data = await response.json();
if (signal.aborted) throw new DOMException("Cancelled", "AbortError");

cards.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix: Python
cards.prompt: Name the invariant protected by this excerpt. It belongs inside the complete solution linked below.
cards.explanation: Check again after awaiting work. An adapter can ignore cancellation, so a pre-request check alone cannot prevent late local publication.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Japanese Alphabet Flashcards
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Always-available hiragana, katakana, sound-change, and beginner word recall for short review sessions.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: English-speaking beginners learning to recognize and read Japanese kana.

cards.title: Hiragana Vowels
cards.prompt: Read あ・い・う・え・お before revealing the romaji.
cards.explanation: The readings are a, i, u, e, o. This vowel order organizes every kana row in the gojūon chart.

cards.title: Hiragana K Row
cards.prompt: Read か・き・く・け・こ aloud from left to right.
cards.explanation: The readings are ka, ki, ku, ke, ko. Keep the fixed vowel order a, i, u, e, o.

cards.title: Hiragana S Row
cards.prompt: Read さ・し・す・せ・そ and notice the irregular label.
cards.explanation: The readings are sa, shi, su, se, so. Learner romaji uses shi instead of a mechanical si.

cards.title: Hiragana T Row
cards.prompt: Read た・ち・つ・て・と and find the two irregular labels.
cards.explanation: The readings are ta, chi, tsu, te, to. Chi and tsu show the pronunciation more clearly than ti and tu.

cards.title: Hiragana N Row
cards.prompt: Read な・に・ぬ・ね・の without looking at a chart.
cards.explanation: The readings are na, ni, nu, ne, no. Compare ぬ and ね by following the loop and final tail.

cards.title: Hiragana H Row
cards.prompt: Read は・ひ・ふ・へ・ほ and recall the special middle sound.
cards.explanation: The readings are ha, hi, fu, he, ho. Japanese fu is lighter than a strongly lip-biting English f.

cards.title: Hiragana M Row
cards.prompt: Read ま・み・む・め・も from shape alone.
cards.explanation: The readings are ma, mi, mu, me, mo. Compare め with ぬ by tracking where the line exits the loop.

cards.title: Hiragana Y Row
cards.prompt: Which three basic sounds are written や・ゆ・よ?
cards.explanation: They are ya, yu, yo. Modern basic Japanese has no separate yi or ye kana in this row.

cards.title: Hiragana R Row
cards.prompt: Read ら・り・る・れ・ろ with one light Japanese r sound.
cards.explanation: The readings are ra, ri, ru, re, ro. The consonant is a brief tongue tap rather than a strong English r.

cards.title: Hiragana Final Row
cards.prompt: Read わ・を・ん and recall where each appears.
cards.explanation: They are wa, object-particle o, and moraic n. を is typed wo even though beginners normally pronounce it o.

cards.title: Compare Ki And Sa
cards.prompt: What visual detail separates き from さ?
cards.explanation: き has two horizontal crossings near the top, while さ has one. Compare the complete shapes, not only the curve.

cards.title: Compare Ru And Ro
cards.prompt: Which one closes with a small loop: る or ろ?
cards.explanation: る closes with a small loop at the bottom. ろ keeps the corresponding lower curve open.

cards.title: Dakuten Voices K
cards.prompt: Read the change か → が and name both sounds.
cards.explanation: か is ka. Adding dakuten voices the consonant, producing が ga and throat vibration.

cards.title: The Circle Makes P
cards.prompt: What does the small circle do in は → ぱ?
cards.explanation: Handakuten changes h-row kana to p sounds. は ha becomes ぱ pa; the same rule gives pi, pu, pe, po.

cards.title: Small Tsu Holds
cards.prompt: Contrast きて kite with きって kitte.
cards.explanation: Small っ creates a brief closure and doubles the following consonant in romaji and common IME input.

cards.title: Small Yo Contracts
cards.prompt: Contrast きよ ki-yo with きょ kyo.
cards.explanation: Full-size よ begins a new mora. Small ょ combines with the preceding i-row kana into one contracted sound.

cards.title: Long A Changes Meaning
cards.prompt: Which is grandmother: おばさん or おばあさん?
cards.explanation: おばあさん obaasan is grandmother. The extra あ lengthens the vowel; おばさん obasan means aunt.

cards.title: Katakana Vowels
cards.prompt: Read ア・イ・ウ・エ・オ using the sounds you already know.
cards.explanation: They are a, i, u, e, o. Katakana changes the shapes, not the underlying five-vowel system.

cards.title: Katakana K Row
cards.prompt: Read カ・キ・ク・ケ・コ from left to right.
cards.explanation: The readings are ka, ki, ku, ke, ko. Connect each sound to its hiragana partner only as a temporary bridge.

cards.title: Katakana S Row
cards.prompt: Read サ・シ・ス・セ・ソ and identify shi.
cards.explanation: The readings are sa, shi, su, se, so. シ is shi and belongs in the i position of the row.

cards.title: Katakana T Row
cards.prompt: Read タ・チ・ツ・テ・ト and identify chi and tsu.
cards.explanation: The readings are ta, chi, tsu, te, to. The sound pattern exactly matches the hiragana t-row.

cards.title: Katakana N Row
cards.prompt: Read ナ・ニ・ヌ・ネ・ノ without romaji.
cards.explanation: The readings are na, ni, nu, ne, no. ノ is a single falling stroke and appears inside many loanwords.

cards.title: Katakana H Row
cards.prompt: Read ハ・ヒ・フ・ヘ・ホ and identify fu.
cards.explanation: The readings are ha, hi, fu, he, ho. フ is a one-stroke fu, often confused with ワ or ウ at first.

cards.title: Katakana M Row
cards.prompt: Read マ・ミ・ム・メ・モ from shape alone.
cards.explanation: The readings are ma, mi, mu, me, mo. ミ has three descending horizontal strokes; ム begins with a triangle-like form.

cards.title: Katakana Y Row
cards.prompt: Read the three basic y-row symbols ヤ・ユ・ヨ.
cards.explanation: They are ya, yu, yo. ユ has two strokes and ヨ has three horizontal levels.

cards.title: Katakana R Row
cards.prompt: Read ラ・リ・ル・レ・ロ with a light tongue tap.
cards.explanation: The readings are ra, ri, ru, re, ro. ロ is the box-shaped ro; do not confuse it with the kanji 口 without context.

cards.title: Katakana Final Row
cards.prompt: Read ワ・ヲ・ン and recall the modern sound of ヲ.
cards.explanation: They are wa, usually o, and moraic n. Katakana ヲ is uncommon in ordinary beginner loanwords.

cards.title: Shi Or Tsu
cards.prompt: Compare シ and ツ: which one has more horizontal short strokes?
cards.explanation: シ shi has short strokes that sit more horizontally. ツ tsu has short strokes that stand more vertically.

cards.title: So Or N
cards.prompt: Compare ソ and ン: which long stroke rises from lower left?
cards.explanation: ン n rises from lower left. ソ so begins higher and falls down toward the left; stroke direction is the clue.

cards.title: Long Vowel Mark
cards.prompt: How does ー affect the sound of コーヒー?
cards.explanation: The mark extends the preceding vowel. コー is koo and ヒー is hii, giving koohii, coffee.

cards.title: Read A Loanword
cards.prompt: Read コーヒー one kana and sound extension at a time.
cards.explanation: コ ko + ー long o + ヒ hi + ー long i gives koohii, the Japanese loanword for coffee.

cards.title: Read Hotel
cards.prompt: Read ホテル before using the familiar English word as a clue.
cards.explanation: ホ ho + テ te + ル ru gives hoteru. Japanese loanwords follow Japanese mora timing rather than English spelling.

cards.title: Read Restaurant
cards.prompt: Break レストラン into kana-sized beats.
cards.explanation: レ re + ス su + ト to + ラ ra + ン n gives resutoran, restaurant.

cards.title: Written Ha, Spoken Wa
cards.prompt: Why is こんばんは read konbanwa but typed konbanha?
cards.explanation: The final は is the topic particle. Learner romaji shows its spoken wa; the IME keys create the written kana ha.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Mermaid Diagram Authoring Scrolling Review
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Review Mermaid syntax, diagram selection, debugging, and readability one screen at a time.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Developers and technical writers learning to read, create, and maintain Mermaid diagrams.

cards.title: Declaration Comes First
cards.prompt: The first meaningful line selects the Mermaid grammar for every statement that follows.
cards.explanation: Use declarations such as flowchart, sequenceDiagram, classDiagram, stateDiagram-v2, or erDiagram before writing relationships.

cards.title: IDs Are Not Labels
cards.prompt: Keep source IDs short and stable while visible labels explain the domain idea.
cards.explanation: In Gateway[API gateway], edges reuse Gateway. The human-facing API gateway label can evolve without changing every relationship.

cards.title: Direction Guides Layout
cards.prompt: LR, TD, TB, RL, and BT request a reading direction rather than fixed coordinates.
cards.explanation: Mermaid's layout engine positions nodes. Authors describe relationships and a preferred direction instead of placing pixels manually.

cards.title: Label Decision Outcomes
cards.prompt: A decision reads faster when every outgoing edge names its outcome.
cards.explanation: The diamond asks one question while Yes and No live on the relationships that represent the possible answers.

cards.title: Group Real Boundaries
cards.prompt: Use subgraphs for ownership, trust, deployment, or domain boundaries—not decoration.
cards.explanation: A named boundary should help the reader reason about responsibility or communication across it.

cards.title: Sequence Means Time
cards.prompt: Read sequence participants across the top and messages from top to bottom.
cards.explanation: Sequence diagrams answer who communicates at each point in a scenario; they are not static dependency maps.

cards.title: Sequence Control Blocks
cards.prompt: Choose alt for alternatives, loop for repetition, and par for concurrent work.
cards.explanation: Each block communicates a different runtime rule; using the precise block reduces prose and ambiguity.
cards.code:
alt Approved
  API-->>Web: 201
else Rejected
  API-->>Web: 409
end

cards.title: Class Diagrams Are Static
cards.prompt: Class diagrams show types, members, inheritance, composition, and dependencies.
cards.explanation: They explain structure independent of one request. Use a sequence diagram when message order is the real question.

cards.title: State Means Legal Next
cards.prompt: A state diagram makes lifecycle transitions and forbidden paths reviewable.
cards.explanation: Durable conditions belong in states; temporary calls and responses belong in actions or sequence messages.

cards.title: Read Crow's Foot
cards.prompt: Exactly one customer may own zero or more orders in this relationship.
cards.explanation: The customer-side double bar means exactly one; the order-side circle and crow's foot mean zero or many.

cards.title: Schedules Become Stale
cards.prompt: A Gantt diagram is a maintained documentation snapshot, not a project-management backend.
cards.explanation: Assign ownership and review dates, durations, and dependencies whenever the underlying plan changes.

cards.title: Journey Scores Need Context
cards.prompt: A journey score is an author judgment unless its measurement source is named.
cards.explanation: Use the 1-to-5 scale consistently and avoid presenting illustrative sentiment as product analytics.

cards.title: Pie Needs A Whole
cards.prompt: Use pie charts for a few categories that form one meaningful total.
cards.explanation: Time series, negative values, and many similar slices need an axis-based chart or table instead.

cards.title: Mindmaps Use Indentation
cards.prompt: Whitespace defines hierarchy in a Mermaid mindmap.
cards.explanation: Consistent indentation is semantic. Use a flowchart instead when branches need explicit arrows or decisions.

cards.title: Timeline Is Not Gantt
cards.prompt: Use timeline for chronology; use Gantt when durations and dependencies matter.
cards.explanation: Both involve time, but only the Gantt grammar models scheduled work and dependency-driven starts.

cards.title: Reduce Before Repairing
cards.prompt: How would you isolate one syntax error inside a large Mermaid block?
cards.explanation: Keep the declaration and one valid statement, then restore lines until the first failing addition identifies the parser boundary.

cards.title: One Question Per Diagram
cards.prompt: What is the fastest way to improve a diagram that tries to show the entire architecture?
cards.explanation: Split it into focused views with explicit questions and consistent abstraction levels instead of adding more color or smaller text.

cards.title: Test The Host Version
cards.prompt: A diagram working in a current editor may fail in an application with an older Mermaid dependency.
cards.explanation: Version-sensitive and experimental grammars must be tested with the same package version, configuration, and security mode as production.

passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: Product Engineering Interview Briefs
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Twelve quick reviews for preview races, durable job correctness, role fit, and credible ownership stories.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: Engineers reviewing before a product engineering interview.

cards.title: Interview: Supersede
cards.prompt: A is active; B then C are submitted before A settles. What should run next?
cards.explanation: Run C after A settles, and suppress A’s obsolete result. The bounded pending slot retains only C. Starting both increases concurrency beyond the contract; keeping A as the visible answer ignores current intent. Completion order cannot determine which input the artist now wants.

cards.title: Interview: Abort
cards.prompt: The provider ignores AbortSignal and resolves after dispose. What prevents a stale render?
cards.explanation: A disposed/revision guard before every UI callback. Cancellation is a request to cooperating operations. A guard still prevents late local callbacks when cancellation is ignored; changing loading state cannot cancel an operation or prove remote work stopped.

cards.title: Interview: Error
cards.prompt: A fails after B was submitted. What should the coordinator do?
cards.explanation: Suppress A’s obsolete error and continue with B. Errors need the same revision guard as results: A no longer describes current intent. The slot must be released in finally so B can run; otherwise one old failure blocks all future work.

cards.title: Interview: Deadline
cards.prompt: The active adapter never settles. Which statement is accurate?
cards.explanation: The baseline blocks; a timeout alone does not prove remote work stopped. Finally runs when control leaves the awaited operation, not after an implicit timeout. Promise.race changes which promise you await; it does not stop the remote operation. Define deadline, cancellation, and capacity policy explicitly.

cards.title: Interview: Uncertain
cards.prompt: A provider finished an export; the worker crashed before recording success. What is the safest retry plan?
cards.explanation: Before repeating the effect, reconcile via a stable provider key or operation ID where supported. Redelivery proves the message needs handling, not that the external effect failed. Otherwise keep the uncertainty explicit; neither blind retries nor invented success preserve correctness.

cards.title: Interview: Outbox
cards.prompt: The API writes a job, then crashes before publishing its queue message. Which design closes this gap?
cards.explanation: Commit the job, credit reservation, and outbox record atomically so dispatch intent survives a crash. Publishing first can create work without an accepted job or reservation. A tab cannot preserve the backend acceptance contract.

cards.title: Interview: Idempotency
cards.prompt: Two workspaces reuse the same idempotency key. What is the correct boundary?
cards.explanation: Scope the key to the workspace and compare the request fingerprint. Tenant scope prevents unrelated requests colliding or leaking results. A body fingerprint detects changed requests under the same key. Prompt text omits workspace, input revision, model, and configuration identity.

cards.title: Interview: Fencing
cards.prompt: Worker A pauses, its lease expires, and worker B commits success. A resumes. What protects the result?
cards.explanation: A guarded state transition with the current attempt/fencing token. A lease can expire while its previous holder is still running. The commit must validate attempt ownership and state/version, so stale workers cannot overwrite B. Last-write-wins is unsafe for results and ledger transitions.

cards.title: Interview: Evidence
cards.prompt: A generic interview site lists likely company questions without candidate provenance. How should you use it?
cards.explanation: Treat these as optional, inferred practice material, not candidate evidence of the company’s actual questions. They establish neither the exact interview loop nor a contradiction with a specific briefing. Confirm logistics directly and prioritize primary role and product material.

cards.title: Interview: Role
cards.prompt: A product engineering role combines frontend and collaboration work with durable jobs. How should preparation change?
cards.explanation: Include frontend state, rendering, product judgment, and collaboration boundaries. The role spans product surfaces and reliability, so the interview preparation should connect them. Backend-only study misses explicit qualifications; syntax memorization alone cannot explain state ownership or user-visible correctness.

cards.title: Interview: Rate
cards.prompt: Your story says traffic grew from 500 to 50,000 RPM. Which statement is accurate?
cards.explanation: That is 100×, about 8.3 to 833 requests/second; define what was measured. Divide requests per minute by 60 and calculate the ratio as 50,000/500. Explain peak versus sustained, ingress versus processed events, and success rate so a capacity claim remains meaningful and defensible.

cards.title: Interview: Recovery
cards.prompt: Tests and a build pass after an incident fix. What can you honestly claim?
cards.explanation: Code validation passed. The final pruned runtime’s startup, deployment, and customer recovery each need separate evidence. Name unknown impact. Local dependencies can hide packaging failures.
