passiveFlashcardFeeds.title: RTK Query Interview Briefs
passiveFlashcardFeeds.summary: Twenty-one concise review cards covering query mechanics, cache scope, errors, persistence, modern APIs, and production judgment.
passiveFlashcardFeeds.audience: React and TypeScript engineers rehearsing concise RTK Query interview answers.

cards.title: Foundations and Request Ownership: Same Key
cards.prompt: Two panels call getAuthor with the same ID in the same API/store. What should happen?
cards.explanation: They share the cache entry and an in-flight request because the endpoint and serialized argument identify the entry. Hook count does not require duplicate HTTP calls, and React element keys do not define RTK cache identity.

cards.title: Foundations and Request Ownership: Current Data
cards.prompt: Switching author A to B must not show A while B loads. Which hook field fits?
cards.explanation: currentData, with explicit loading and error handling for B. currentData belongs to the current argument. data may retain a previous argument result; copying it once creates a stale second owner and does not protect identity changes.

cards.title: Foundations and Request Ownership: State Owner
cards.prompt: Where should an unsaved multi-step editing draft live?
cards.explanation: In intentional client state with its own save/reset and persistence policy. Drafts have a different owner and lifetime from server snapshots. Directly mutating cached results breaks the state contract; Redux Toolkit can model client workflows with ordinary slices.

cards.title: Cache Identity and Invalidation: Retention
cards.prompt: The final subscriber leaves at t=40s with keepUnusedDataFor: 60. No one returns. When is eviction expected?
cards.explanation: Around t=100s. Unused retention starts after the final unsubscribe, when the subscription count reaches zero. It is not measured from fetch time, and cache eviction does not require a mutation.

cards.title: Cache Identity and Invalidation: Hidden Page
cards.prompt: Deleting a record on page one shifts page three, which never provided that record tag. What helps?
cards.explanation: Invalidate a scoped collection or PARTIAL-LIST tag as well as relevant entity tags. A collection dependency covers membership/count changes outside a visible page. An unprovided entity tag will not match that page, and longer retention cannot correct stale membership.

cards.title: Cache Identity and Invalidation: Headers
cards.prompt: Tenant changes affect only prepareHeaders; the endpoint arguments stay equal. What is missing?
cards.explanation: Explicit cache scope and account-transition cleanup for identity-dependent data. Headers are not automatically default key dimensions. Model non-secret identity scope and clear protected state on transition; random keys waste reuse and fail to express the actual data contract.

cards.title: Mutations and Error Recovery: Unwrap
cards.prompt: A save handler uses await trigger(args) then always shows Saved. A handled 400 still shows success. What fixes the flow?
cards.explanation: Use unwrap with try/catch, or inspect the returned error result explicitly. Handled errors can be returned in the trigger result; unwrap exposes promise-style rejection. fixedCacheKey shares mutation state and does not alter HTTP error semantics.

cards.title: Mutations and Error Recovery: Patch Race
cards.prompt: Edit one patches A to B, edit two patches C, then edit one fails. Why is naive undo risky?
cards.explanation: The earlier inverse patch can overwrite newer intent; serialize or reconcile with server state. Inverse patches describe local changes, not distributed write ordering. Immer cannot order server operations, and an older patch does not automatically account for later success.

cards.title: Mutations and Error Recovery: Missing Entry
cards.prompt: updateQueryData targets an endpoint/argument with no cached entry. What happens?
cards.explanation: It does not create the missing entry; deliberate upsert may be needed. updateQueryData targets an existing exact entry and does not initiate a fetch or patch by tags. upsertQueryData is the explicit creation/replacement mechanism.

cards.title: Persistence and the Loading Incident: Orphaned Pending
cards.prompt: After process death, a raw persisted pending entry returns but no request exists. What explains the loader?
cards.explanation: Restored execution metadata can block initiation without restoring the actual request. Serialized pending state does not recreate a promise or prove server activity. The thunk can reject a duplicate initiation for that key even when the original client request no longer exists.

cards.title: Persistence and the Loading Incident: Two Paths
cards.prompt: Which statement about RTK 2.2.8 and 2.12.0 rehydration is accurate?
cards.explanation: The inspected extractRehydrationInfo reducer path filters pending entries in both versions. Raw state restoration can bypass it, so upgrading alone cannot guarantee correct custom persistence wiring.

cards.title: Persistence and the Loading Incident: Both Directions
cards.prompt: Why filter pending records both before writing and after reading old storage?
cards.explanation: Writes prevent recurrence; reads repair already persisted bad entries. Both directions cover distinct populations: future snapshots and existing installations. A write filter does not itself migrate old data; a read repair does not prevent malformed snapshots from being written.

cards.title: Modern APIs and Version Traps: Page Identity
cards.prompt: An infinite feed varies by tenant and topic and navigates using a cursor. How should it be modeled?
cards.explanation: Tenant/topic in queryArg; cursor in pageParam. The collection identity stays stable across pages while the page parameter advances. Dropping tenant/topic creates collisions, and per-page API slices fragment subscriptions and invalidation.

cards.title: Modern APIs and Version Traps: Schema Version
cards.prompt: Which version first added Standard Schema validation to RTK Query?
cards.explanation: Standard Schema support arrived in RTK 2.7.0. The case-study 2.2.8 baseline predates it; 2.12.0 includes later fixes and improvements rather than introducing the original schema API.

cards.title: Modern APIs and Version Traps: Refetch Pages
cards.prompt: In RTK 2.11+, what does refetchCachedPages: false do on an infinite-query refetch?
cards.explanation: It refetches the first cached page and shrinks the retained cache to one page. It does not preserve all later pages and does not disable the endpoint; scroll behavior needs an explicit product policy.

cards.title: Production Architecture and Testing: Inject
cards.prompt: Two feature files need coordinated Author invalidation. What is the usual starting point?
cards.explanation: Inject endpoints into a shared base API and register its middleware once. Endpoint injection preserves the shared cache/tag namespace. Equal tag names across separate APIs do not coordinate them, and duplicate middleware registration is not required.

cards.title: Production Architecture and Testing: Selector
cards.prompt: selectFromResult returns a newly filtered array each time. Why can rerenders persist?
cards.explanation: The selected array reference changes; memoize derived collections or select stable values. The returned fields are compared shallowly. A fresh nested array changes a field reference; a new outer object with stable fields is expected, and real selected changes must still rerender.

cards.title: Production Architecture and Testing: Stream Lifetime
cards.prompt: Which lifecycle is suitable for a stream tied to cached data?
cards.explanation: onCacheEntryAdded with validated events and cleanup after cacheEntryRemoved. Cache-entry lifecycle work can own a stream and clean it up. Render-driven sockets leak/duplicate work; a permanently pending HTTP query confuses query completion and can delay invalidation.

cards.title: Mock Interview and Code Review: Priority
cards.prompt: A review finds stale spinners and cross-account cached data. What is the strongest first priority?
cards.explanation: Fix and test identity boundaries while preserving server authorization. Cross-account display requires urgent scope correction and regression coverage. Animation changes cannot fix data isolation, and server authorization remains mandatory regardless of cache keys.

cards.title: Mock Interview and Code Review: Stale Layer
cards.prompt: Invalidation triggers an HTTP request, but its response contains old data. What next?
cards.explanation: The observed request narrows the problem. Old response data points upstream: inspect server consistency and HTTP/cache layers. If the response is correct, inspect client selectors. Broad repeated invalidation is not a diagnosis.

cards.title: Mock Interview and Code Review: Modern Tradeoff
cards.prompt: An interviewer asks about a newer RTK API. Which answer shows useful judgment?
cards.explanation: Explain infinite query page identity and the scroll consequences of collapsing a refetch to one page. A concrete mechanism and product tradeoff demonstrate understanding. Version recitation alone is weak, and modern API support does not validate an application’s custom persistence path.

questions.title: Palindrome Pairs
questions.summary: Find all ordered pairs of words that form a palindrome when concatenated.
questions.prompt: Given a list of unique words, return every pair of distinct indexes where words[i] plus words[j] is a palindrome.

examples.explanation: bat + tab and tab + bat are palindromes.

constraints: Pairs are ordered and indexes must be distinct.
Words are unique ASCII strings; the empty string is allowed.

solutionTracks.title: Hash Map Split Check
solutionTracks.summary: Try every split in every word and use a reversed-word map to find a partner for the non-palindrome side.

steps.title: Map words to indexes
steps.explanation: A hash map finds whether the reverse of a needed fragment exists.

steps.title: Split every word
steps.explanation: Each cut creates a left and right fragment. One fragment may be the palindrome middle.

steps.title: Emit both orientations
steps.explanation: If the left is palindrome, a reversed right can go before; if the right is palindrome, a reversed left can go after.

solutionTracks.explanation: For word A plus word B to be a palindrome, the unmatched portion after mirrored comparison must already be palindromic. Splitting enumerates every possible unmatched portion.

complexity.space: O(n k + p), including p output pairs

solutionTracks.title: Pairwise Palindrome Baseline
solutionTracks.summary: Try every ordered pair and test the concatenation with two pointers.

steps.title: Enumerate distinct indexes
steps.explanation: Try each ordered pair i, j with i != j.

steps.title: Check the concatenation
steps.explanation: Compare mirrored characters; reject at the first mismatch.

steps.title: Collect and compare
steps.explanation: Keep accepted pairs and use this baseline as an oracle for an optimized solution.

solutionTracks.explanation: Every legal ordered pair is inspected once. Two pointers accept exactly the concatenations that read the same in both directions. This is a clear baseline to establish correctness before discussing the split-and-hash optimization.

complexity.time: O(n² k), maximum word length k

questions.title: In-Memory File System
questions.summary: Design a small file system API with directory listing and file content operations.
questions.prompt: Implement ls, mkdir, addContentToFile, and readContentFromFile for an in-memory file system rooted at slash.

examples.explanation: The file c is inside directory /a/b.

constraints: Directory listings should be returned in lexicographic order.
Paths are normalized absolute paths; reads and listings address existing paths. No file/directory conflicts, dot segments, deletion, or permissions are required.

diagrams.title: Path tree
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  R[/] --> A[a]
  A --> B[b]
  B --> C[c file]

solutionTracks.title: Path Trie
solutionTracks.summary: Represent directories as trie nodes and keep optional file contents on nodes that are files.

steps.title: Split paths
steps.explanation: Break a path into non-empty parts so each part becomes one trie edge.

steps.title: Create directories lazily
steps.explanation: mkdir and addContent create missing nodes along the path.

steps.title: Separate listing behavior
steps.explanation: ls returns a single filename for file nodes or sorted child names for directory nodes.

solutionTracks.explanation: A trie matches the hierarchy of a file system: each node owns its children and possibly file content. Walking path parts reaches exactly the requested location. Let L be path length, d the number of path parts, b the maximum siblings, c the listed children, and F the resulting file size. The trie uses expected O(L) hash lookup in Python/TS or O(L + d log b) TreeMap lookup in Java. Flat-map mkdir constructs cumulative path strings and can cost O(L²); listings sort in Python/TS (O(c log c) comparisons), while Java stores children sorted. Immutable-string append can copy O(F) characters in Python/TS; Java StringBuilder append is amortized in added characters. Returning file text may cost O(F). Reads/listings assume existing paths.

complexity.time: Path traversal plus listing/output cost; see language-specific explanation

solutionTracks.title: Flat Path Maps
solutionTracks.summary: Store directories and files in separate maps keyed by full path for a compact MVP implementation.

steps.title: Track directory children
steps.explanation: A directory map stores sorted names for each directory path.

steps.title: Track file content
steps.explanation: A file map stores content by complete file path.

questions.title: Reverse A Linked List
questions.summary: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
questions.prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list in place and return the new head node.

examples.explanation: Every next pointer is redirected to the previous node.

constraints: Do not allocate a second list in the iterative solution.

solutionTracks.title: Iterative Pointer Reversal
solutionTracks.summary: Walk the list once while redirecting each node to point at the previous node instead of the next node.

steps.title: Hold previous and current
steps.explanation: Previous starts empty and current starts at the head.

steps.title: Save next before rewiring
steps.explanation: Store current.next before overwriting it so the rest of the list is not lost.

steps.title: Advance both pointers
steps.explanation: Move previous to current and current to the saved next node until the list ends.

solutionTracks.explanation: At every step, previous is the head of the already reversed prefix and current is the first node not yet reversed. Rewiring current extends the reversed prefix by one node.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev

java.label: Java

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Reversal
solutionTracks.summary: Let recursion reverse the tail, then attach the current node after its original next node.

steps.title: Find the new head
steps.explanation: When the recursive call reaches the last node, that node becomes the new head.

steps.title: Flip the edge
steps.explanation: After the tail is reversed, current.next.next should point back to current.

steps.title: Break the old edge
steps.explanation: Set current.next to null so the old forward link does not create a cycle.

solutionTracks.explanation: The recursive call returns a fully reversed suffix. Repointing the suffix tail back to the current node adds the current node to the end of that reversed suffix.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def reverse_list_recursive(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_list_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

questions.title: Recursive File Explorer
questions.summary: Combine both supplied tree briefs into a recursive explorer with explicit expansion-state behavior.
questions.prompt: Render nested file/folder mock data using FileExplorer and a recursive FileItem. Support expanding and collapsing folders, an empty-data message, indentation, and vertical hierarchy lines for expanded children.

examples.input: src folder contains components folder containing FileExplorer.tsx.
examples.output: Opening src reveals components; opening components reveals the file one level deeper.
examples.explanation: Closing src hides every descendant. On reopening, descendant expansion follows the selected approach’s documented ownership policy.

constraints: Use globally unique stable IDs, not filenames, as keys.
Retain recursive FileItem rendering in all three approaches.
Specify whether child expansion resets or persists when an ancestor closes.
Data is a finite acyclic tree; cycle validation is a follow-up for untrusted input.

evaluation.intent: Combine both supplied tree briefs into a recursive explorer with explicit expansion-state behavior. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Use the explicit node type to handle empty folders.
Explain local unmount/reset behavior versus controlled expansion.
Match indentation and hierarchy lines to nested structure.

acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Render nested file/folder mock data using FileExplorer and a recursive FileItem. Support expanding and collapsing folders, an empty-data message, indentation, and vertical hierarchy lines for expanded children.

acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs

solutionTracks.title: Recursive local state
solutionTracks.summary: Let each folder component own its expanded flag for the shortest implementation.

steps.title: State the tree contract
steps.explanation: Use finite acyclic mock data, globally unique IDs, and a file/folder discriminated type. A folder may have no children.

steps.title: Render one node recursively
steps.explanation: FileItem displays a file name or a folder button. Render child FileItems only when the folder is open.

steps.title: Choose expansion ownership
steps.explanation: Use one boolean per mounted folder. Closing an ancestor removes its children; their local state resets on reopening.

steps.title: Check empty and nested cases
steps.explanation: Render a no-data message for an empty root list and an empty-folder message for a folder without children. Use nested lists and left borders for hierarchy.

steps.title: Explain limits
steps.explanation: Recursive depth consumes stack space. For untrusted or extremely deep trees, validate cycles and consider a different traversal strategy; that is a follow-up, not this mock-data contract.

solutionTracks.explanation: A recursive renderer matches the tree definition: display the current node, then apply the same rule to each visible child. Stable IDs distinguish equal filenames. Rendering only expanded descendants prevents collapsed content from appearing, while nested lists encode the hierarchy.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Local expansion resets after ancestor unmounting; controlled and normalized versions preserve it. Both policies are valid when stated explicitly.
Do not use names as keys, mutate a Set in place, or infer a folder from nonempty children. Empty folders still have type folder.
The simple recursive visible-row helper may copy descendant results at each level: O(v × h) worst case. Normalized traversal appends into one accumulator.

complexity.space: O(n + e + v + h) including data, expansion, rows, and stack

questions.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips
questions.summary: Model selection and derived filtering while preserving disabled options, keyboard access, and dismissal behavior.
questions.prompt: Build a filterable multi-select. Selecting an enabled option adds a removable chip, clears the input, and removes that option from the dropdown. Show matching disabled options as unavailable. Close outside the component and show No results when nothing matches.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.input: Type "script", choose TypeScript, then remove its chip.
examples.output: TypeScript becomes selected, input clears, and it disappears from results; removal restores it.
examples.explanation: The dropdown is derived from current selection and query, so the two views cannot drift.

constraints: Match anywhere in the label, case-insensitively.
Use explicit IDs; selected options cannot be duplicated.
Disabled options must be visible when matching and rejected by the model.
Support Tab/Enter/Space, Escape, outside pointer dismissal, and visible focus.

evaluation.intent: Model selection and derived filtering while preserving disabled options, keyboard access, and dismissal behavior. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Derive the filtered list rather than storing redundant results.
Reject disabled options even if selection is called programmatically.
Explain focus movement and remove global listeners during cleanup.

acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Build a filterable multi-select. Selecting an enabled option adds a removable chip, clears the input, and removes that option from the dropdown. Show matching disabled options as unavailable. Close outside the component and show No results when nothing matches.

acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs

solutionTracks.title: Local state and derived options
solutionTracks.summary: Keep selection, query, and open state together; derive visible options on every render.

steps.title: Specify selection identity
steps.explanation: Assign stable option IDs. Selected IDs and query are state; the filtered dropdown is derived, not separately synchronized state.

steps.title: Enforce rules in the model
steps.explanation: Case-insensitive substring matching excludes selected IDs. Disabled options remain visible when matching, but selection is rejected in the transition itself.

steps.title: Compose chips and input
steps.explanation: Place removable buttons and the input inside one visual field. Selecting clears the query; removal makes an option available again.

steps.title: Handle focus and dismissal
steps.explanation: Native buttons provide Tab/Enter/Space operation. Close on outside pointer events, focus leaving the component, and Escape. Clean up the document listener.

steps.title: Explain the chosen organization
steps.explanation: Local state is the baseline. A reducer clarifies growing event rules. A controlled hook helps reuse the model. All three have the same filtering complexity.

solutionTracks.explanation: The visible list is a pure function of options, selected IDs, and query, so removing or selecting cannot leave a stale dropdown. Selection checks run inside the model as well as in disabled buttons. A single transition clears the query and adds the chip atomically.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Do not present these organization alternatives as three faster filtering algorithms: each scans the option labels.
Native labeled inputs and buttons are intentional here. A full ARIA combobox would also require its complete arrow-key and active-descendant behavior.
Use IDs rather than labels for identity. The supplied labels are unique, but that need not hold for future data.

complexity.time: O(n × L + s) filtering; O(n + s) selection, n options, L label length, s selected IDs
complexity.space: O(n + s) derived options and selection

questions.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix
questions.summary: Fetch user counts, handle partial failures, and place results in stable unique cells despite out-of-order requests.
questions.prompt: Fetch up to three users from /userList, retrieve each user’s public owned repository count, and display the users in distinct random positions of a 3×3 grid. Keep positions stable while results arrive and report errors per user.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.input: Ada succeeds with 103 repositories; Grace fails; Linus succeeds with 2.
examples.output: Three unique cells retain their assigned users; Grace shows an error while Ada and Linus show their counts.
examples.explanation: Failures and completion order do not change identity or placement.

constraints: Use mocked asynchronous data in the playground.
The corrected GitHub endpoint is /users/{username}/repos?type=owner; follow every page.
Deduplicate usernames case-insensitively as an authored practice rule.
A reload starts a new assignment; unrelated renders and individual responses do not.

evaluation.intent: Fetch user counts, handle partial failures, and place results in stable unique cells despite out-of-order requests. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Notice the source URL typo and pagination limit.
Separate fetching, placement, and rendering.
Prove stale-response suppression with a mock that ignores cancellation.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs
redFlags.explanation: Separate model computation, immutable copying, network latency, and rendering before comparing approaches.

solutionTracks.title: Sequential requests
solutionTracks.summary: Start with the easiest request order to explain and debug, accepting additive latency.

steps.title: Clarify what count means
steps.explanation: Count public owned repositories. Correct the URL to /users/{username}/repos and page through the complete response; private repositories require a different authorization contract.

steps.title: Assign cells before requests
steps.explanation: Fetch up to three usernames, deduplicate case-insensitively, and sample unique positions from nine cells. Store assignments before repository results arrive.

steps.title: Choose request orchestration
steps.explanation: Fetch each user in sequence; capture a failure and continue so one error does not hide other users.

steps.title: Protect lifecycle updates
steps.explanation: Pass cancellation to the adapter and check it again after awaits. On reload or unmount, cancel the old generation so even an adapter that ignores abort cannot publish stale results.

steps.title: Demonstrate adverse outcomes
steps.explanation: Use mock pages with more than 100 repositories, a rate-limit error, and late responses. Show stable positions and successful users alongside failures.

solutionTracks.explanation: Sampling cells without replacement prevents collisions. Binding each request to its preassigned user/index prevents completion order from moving users. Pagination counts every returned page; cancellation checks guard publication even if a transport ignores cancellation. Per-user errors remain data rather than wiping out unrelated successes.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: The playground uses deterministic mocks and never calls GitHub. The adapter can use fetch in a local experiment; never embed tokens in browser code.
A paginated listing is not a transactional snapshot. Concurrent repository creation/deletion can affect a live count; tests use fixed pages.
Bounded concurrency is an extension for quota pressure. With at most three users, the parallel baseline is usually sufficient.
Cancellation prevents stale local publication; it does not prove remote work stopped.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.summary: Count contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target value.
questions.prompt: Given an array of integers and a target k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose values sum to k.

examples.explanation: The first two and last two values both sum to 2.

constraints: Values may be negative, so sliding window is not sufficient.

solutionTracks.title: Prefix Sum Counts
solutionTracks.summary: Count previous prefix sums so each current prefix can identify how many earlier starts produce the target sum.

steps.title: Maintain running sum
steps.explanation: The sum of a subarray ending at the current index is current prefix minus an earlier prefix.

steps.title: Look for prefix minus k
steps.explanation: If current minus target has appeared before, each occurrence starts a valid subarray.

steps.title: Record current prefix
steps.explanation: After counting matches, add the current prefix to support future endings.

solutionTracks.explanation: For any end index, subarray sum equals prefix[end] minus prefix[start before]. Rearranging gives the exact earlier prefix value needed for target k.

solutionTracks.summary: Build prefix sums first, then compare every start and end pair to make the target relationship explicit.

steps.title: Build prefix array
steps.explanation: prefix[i] stores the sum of every item before index i.

steps.title: Try all ranges
steps.explanation: For every start and end, compute prefix[end] minus prefix[start].

steps.title: Count target ranges
steps.explanation: Increment the answer whenever that range sum equals k.

solutionTracks.explanation: This version is slower but useful for deriving the optimized formula. Prefix sums make each candidate range sum O(1) instead of rescanning the range.

questions.title: Word Ladder
questions.summary: Find the shortest one-letter-at-a-time transformation from one word to another.
questions.prompt: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence where each step changes one letter and remains in the dictionary.

examples.explanation: hit, hot, dot, dog, cog has five words.

constraints: Every transformation has equal cost.
Words contain lowercase ASCII letters and have equal length. Identical begin/end returns 1, including when absent from the dictionary.

solutionTracks.title: Breadth-First Word Search
solutionTracks.summary: Treat words as graph nodes and use BFS because every one-letter transformation has equal cost.

steps.title: Queue the start word
steps.explanation: BFS starts with the begin word at distance one and a set of unused dictionary words.

steps.title: Generate neighbors
steps.explanation: For each position, try replacing it with every letter and keep candidates that are in the dictionary.

steps.title: Stop at target
steps.explanation: The first time BFS reaches the end word is the shortest transformation length.

solutionTracks.explanation: BFS explores all paths of length d before any path of length d plus one. Because every transformation costs one, the first end-word discovery is optimal.

complexity.time: O(n m² × 26) worst case, including candidate construction/hash cost

solutionTracks.title: Bidirectional BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Search from both begin and end words, always expanding the smaller frontier to reduce the branching work.

steps.title: Keep two frontiers
steps.explanation: One set grows from the begin word and one grows backward from the end word.

steps.title: Expand the smaller side
steps.explanation: Choosing the smaller frontier limits the number of generated one-letter variants.

steps.title: Meet in the middle
steps.explanation: When a generated word exists in the opposite frontier, the two half paths connect.

solutionTracks.explanation: Both searches still use BFS levels, so meeting frontiers gives the shortest path. Expanding the smaller frontier often cuts the explored graph dramatically.

solutionTracks.title: Binary Partition
solutionTracks.summary: Binary search the shorter array for a partition where every left-side value is less than every right-side value.

steps.title: Search shorter array
steps.explanation: Using the shorter array bounds the binary search and makes edge cases easier to control.

steps.title: Balance left size
steps.explanation: Choose the matching partition in the second array so the combined left half has the desired size.

steps.title: Validate boundaries
steps.explanation: When left maximums are not greater than right minimums, the partition gives the median immediately.

solutionTracks.explanation: The correct median partition is the place where the combined left half contains the smaller values and the combined right half contains the larger values. Binary search moves toward that boundary.

questions.summary: Count connected groups of land in a rectangular grid and compare breadth-first with depth-first flood fill.
questions.prompt: Given a rectangular grid containing the character '1' for land and '0' for water, return the number of orthogonally connected islands. Solve it once with breadth-first search and once with depth-first search, then explain the practical tradeoffs.

examples.explanation: The upper-left land cells form one island and the lower-right land cells form another.

constraints: Only horizontal and vertical neighbors are connected.

flowchart LR

solutionTracks.title: BFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Scan for unvisited land, count a new island, then use a queue to mark that entire connected component.

steps.title: Scan every cell
steps.explanation: An unvisited land cell begins a connected component that has not been counted yet.

steps.title: Queue the component
steps.explanation: Mark the starting cell visited and process orthogonal land neighbors in FIFO order.

steps.title: Count each start once
steps.explanation: The outer scan increments only when it finds land that no previous flood fill reached.

solutionTracks.explanation: BFS marks every land cell in one connected component before the scan can count it again. It avoids recursion depth risk, though its queue can grow with a wide island frontier.

solutionTracks.title: DFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Scan for unvisited land, count a new island, then recursively consume that entire connected component.

steps.title: Define the boundary
steps.explanation: Return when a cell is outside the grid, water, or already visited.

steps.title: Explore one branch
steps.explanation: Mark land and recursively visit its four orthogonal neighbors before returning.

steps.title: Count component roots
steps.explanation: Each outer-scan land cell still unseen is the root of one newly counted island.

solutionTracks.explanation: Recursive DFS closely matches the definition of a connected component and is shorter to read. It has the same asymptotic cost as BFS, but one enormous island can overflow the runtime call stack.

questions.title: Shortest Path In A Binary Matrix
questions.summary: Find the minimum number of equal-cost moves through open cells in a square matrix.
questions.prompt: Given a square binary grid, return the length of the shortest clear path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell using eight-direction movement, or -1 when no path exists.

examples.explanation: A diagonal move reaches the destination in a path containing two cells.

constraints: Zero cells are open and one cells are blocked.
Every legal move has equal cost.
The matrix is nonempty and square.

solutionTracks.title: Layered BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Explore all grid positions at one path length before advancing to the next length.

steps.title: Reject blocked endpoints
steps.explanation: No route can exist when either the start or destination cell is blocked.

steps.title: Expand one distance layer
steps.explanation: Queue each unseen open neighbor with a distance one greater than its parent.

steps.title: Return first destination
steps.explanation: BFS guarantees that the first destination removed from the queue has minimum distance.

solutionTracks.explanation: The grid is an unweighted graph because every move costs one. BFS processes paths in nondecreasing length, so it can return as soon as the destination is reached.

solutionTracks.title: In-Place Layer BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Reuse the mutable grid as visited state and count one complete queue layer for each path length.

steps.title: Mark the start
steps.explanation: Change the starting open cell to blocked so it cannot be enqueued again.

steps.title: Process one layer
steps.explanation: Every cell currently in the queue has the same shortest path length from the start.

steps.title: Advance the distance
steps.explanation: After one queue layer finishes, increment the path length before expanding the next layer.

solutionTracks.explanation: This BFS keeps the same shortest-path invariant but stores visited state in the grid. It uses less auxiliary bookkeeping, though mutating caller-owned input must be allowed and stated clearly.

questions.title: Course Schedule
questions.summary: Decide whether every course can be completed by detecting a cycle in the prerequisite graph.
questions.prompt: Given a course count and prerequisite pairs, return whether all courses can be completed. Compare depth-first cycle coloring with breadth-first topological processing.

examples.explanation: Each course requires the other, so neither dependency chain can finish.

constraints: Courses are numbered from zero through course count minus one.
Duplicate prerequisite pairs may be ignored.

solutionTracks.title: DFS Three-Color Cycle Detection
solutionTracks.summary: Color each course unseen, visiting, or complete and reject any edge back to the active DFS path.

steps.title: Enter as visiting
steps.explanation: Mark a course as active before recursively checking every dependent course.

steps.title: Detect a back edge
steps.explanation: An edge to another visiting course closes a directed cycle on the current path.

steps.title: Finish as complete
steps.explanation: After every dependency returns safely, mark the course complete so later searches can reuse the result.

solutionTracks.explanation: A directed cycle exists exactly when DFS reaches a node already on its active path. Complete nodes have already been proven safe and need no repeated exploration.

solutionTracks.title: BFS Kahn Topological Processing
solutionTracks.summary: Queue every course with zero prerequisites and remove completed prerequisite edges until no ready course remains.

steps.title: Count incoming edges
steps.explanation: Indegree records how many unmet prerequisites prevent each course from becoming ready.

steps.title: Queue ready courses
steps.explanation: Every zero-indegree course can be completed immediately and processed in BFS order.

steps.title: Compare processed total
steps.explanation: If all courses are removed, the graph is acyclic; a cycle leaves some indegrees positive.

solutionTracks.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes that have no remaining prerequisites. A directed cycle has no removable starting point inside the cycle, so the final processed count exposes it.

questions.title: Valid Palindrome With One Deletion
questions.summary: Decide whether a string can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
questions.prompt: Given a string, return true when it is already a palindrome or can become one by deleting at most one character.

examples.explanation: Deleting b or c leaves a palindrome.

constraints: Use at most one deletion.
Treat the input as case-sensitive plain characters.
Use ASCII input for identical indexing behavior across these language examples.

solutionTracks.title: Two Pointers With One Skip
solutionTracks.summary: Walk inward and spend the single allowed deletion only when the two boundary characters disagree.

steps.title: Compare boundaries
steps.explanation: Move left and right inward while characters match because the outside of the palindrome is already proven.

steps.title: Branch once on mismatch
steps.explanation: At the first mismatch, test the remaining substring after skipping the left character or the right character.

steps.title: Avoid extra branching
steps.explanation: After the skip is spent, the helper performs a plain palindrome check with no further deletions.

solutionTracks.explanation: Only the first mismatch can require the optional deletion. If skipping either side makes the middle a palindrome then one deletion is enough; otherwise no later decision can repair that boundary mismatch.

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Mismatch Budget
solutionTracks.summary: Model the deletion as a one-use budget and recurse only when the current pair of characters mismatches.

steps.title: Carry the budget
steps.explanation: The helper receives left, right, and whether the deletion has already been used.

steps.title: Recurse on mismatch
steps.explanation: When characters differ and the budget is unused, try consuming it on either side.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def vertical_traversal(root):
    rows = []
    def dfs(node, row, col):
        if not node:
            return
        rows.append((col, row, node.val))
        dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)
        dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)
    dfs(root, 0, 0)
    ans = []
    last_col = None
    for col, row, value in sorted(rows):
        if col != last_col:
            ans.append([])
            last_col = col
        ans[-1].append(value)
    return ans

python.label: Python
python.code:
def longest_distinct(items):
    seen = set()
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, item in enumerate(items):
        while item in seen:
            seen.remove(items[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(item)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

interviewCollections.name: Real-world interviews
interviewCollections.summary: Anonymous exercises adapted from real interview sessions, focused on product judgment, communication, and working frontend code.

questions.title: Generate a Mondrian-style Composition
questions.summary: Scope and build a browser-only React application that creates a fresh, bounded composition from constrained randomness.
questions.prompt: Build a static, browser-only frontend that generates a new Mondrian-style composition on initial page load. Do not add a backend or save data. First agree on the characteristics to imitate, choose an MVP achievable during the interview, and leave extension points for deferred rules. The composition must vary between page loads.
questions.sourceNote: Adapted from a privately supplied real interview brief. The originating company and revealing source URL are intentionally withheld.
constraints: Deliver a working browser-only MVP during a normal interview session.
Generate the composition once on initial load; React rerenders must not silently replace it.
Use only orthogonal divisions, bounded rectangles, consistent dark lines, and a restrained off-white, red, yellow, and blue palette.
Keep every generated region inside the composition and prevent unusably small regions.
Make the composition responsive and keep the generator separate from the renderer.
Explain which characteristics were deliberately deferred and how the design could add them later.

evaluation.intent: Agree on priorities, turn the ambiguous visual request into a small set of deliverable requirements, and implement stable geometry. Leave room for richer composition rules without overbuilding the interview MVP. Perfect art reproduction is secondary.
expectedSignals: Names the visual grammar before coding: orthogonal black lines, unequal rectangles, asymmetric balance, a warm light ground, and sparse primary-color accents.
Negotiates a concrete MVP and explicitly defers secondary traits such as merged regions, line hierarchy, texture, historical-period fidelity, and export.
Models generation as a pure or seed-driven transform so geometry can be inspected and tested independently from React rendering.
Constrains random choices with minimum sizes, weighted colors, bounded coordinates, and a fixed amount of work instead of trusting arbitrary Math.random calls.
Generates once per seed and changes the seed only for initial load or an explicit regenerate action, avoiding render-time instability.
Uses semantic controls, a useful accessible label for the visual output, stable keys, and a responsive composition surface.
Discusses how the selected renderer affects precision, readability, testing, export, and future visual rules.
Communicates tradeoffs while implementing and can identify the next highest-value refinement after the MVP works.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Orthogonal visual grammar
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: The composition is made from horizontal and vertical divisions only; diagonals, circles, arbitrary polygons, and decorative gradients would change the requested visual language.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Consistent dark structure
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Black or near-black lines visibly organize the composition, render above fills where appropriate, and remain consistent enough to read as one system.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Asymmetric rectangles
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Rows, columns, or subdivisions have meaningfully unequal proportions, producing deliberate imbalance rather than a uniform checkerboard.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Restrained weighted palette
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Most area remains warm white or neutral while red, yellow, and blue appear as sparse accents; choosing every color uniformly produces visual noise.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Valid bounded geometry
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Coordinates and dimensions stay inside the canvas, have positive area, respect a practical minimum size, and never overlap unexpectedly.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Stable randomness
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: A composition is created once for a seed and remains stable through unrelated React rerenders; reload or the explicit regenerate control creates the next result.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Responsive and accessible output
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: The artwork scales to mobile and desktop without overflow, the regenerate control is keyboard accessible, and the otherwise abstract visual has an informative accessible name.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Extension seams
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Palette policy, geometry generation, seeded randomness, and rendering are separated well enough to add merged cells, stronger composition heuristics, export, or repeatable seeds later.

redFlags.title: Hardcodes one painting
redFlags.explanation: A fixed arrangement may look convincing but misses the required refresh-time generation and avoids the core modeling problem.

redFlags.title: Randomizes during render
redFlags.explanation: Calling random generation directly in component rendering causes flicker, changes output after unrelated state updates, and behaves especially poorly under React Strict Mode.

redFlags.title: Uses unconstrained geometry
redFlags.explanation: Independent random widths and positions commonly create overlaps, gaps, negative dimensions, or slivers too small to read, showing that invariants were never defined.

redFlags.title: Mutates the DOM directly
redFlags.explanation: Imperative document queries and element mutation fight React ownership, complicate cleanup, and make the generator difficult to test or reuse.

redFlags.title: Overbuilds before an MVP
redFlags.explanation: Starting with a custom canvas engine, physics, image analysis, or a large dependency stack risks finishing nothing and contradicts the explicit scoping portion of the interview.

redFlags.title: Never states a scope
redFlags.explanation: Silently choosing characteristics prevents interviewer collaboration and makes it impossible to judge whether omissions were intentional or accidental.

redFlags.title: Colors every cell uniformly
redFlags.explanation: Equal-probability primary colors create a noisy mosaic instead of the restrained negative space and sparse accents that define the target grammar.

redFlags.title: Assumes one desktop size
redFlags.explanation: Fixed pixel coordinates without a scaling strategy make the deliverable unusable on the mobile-first product and reveal missing layout thinking.

redFlags.title: Omits accessibility
redFlags.explanation: An unlabeled visual and icon-only regeneration control make the experience opaque to assistive technology even though the required semantics are inexpensive.

redFlags.title: Entangles model and renderer
redFlags.explanation: Geometry hidden inside JSX or CSS string concatenation cannot be validated independently and makes future renderers or composition rules costly.

redFlags.title: Cannot explain tradeoffs
redFlags.explanation: A polished artifact without discussion of renderer choice, deferred rules, or failure modes misses the communication and design dimensions of the rubric.

solutionTracks.title: Weighted CSS Grid
solutionTracks.summary: Generate unequal fractional tracks and a sparse weighted palette, then let CSS Grid own all layout and line spacing.

steps.title: Lock the MVP grammar
steps.explanation: Choose unequal rows and columns, one consistent black gap, a warm neutral ground, and exactly three primary-color accents as the deliverable subset.

steps.title: Make randomness repeatable
steps.explanation: Create a small seeded random function so one seed always yields the same track weights, accent positions, and test result.

steps.title: Generate constrained tracks
steps.explanation: Use bounded positive fractional weights rather than independent pixel positions; CSS Grid then guarantees full coverage without overlap.

steps.title: Bias the palette
steps.explanation: Start every cell as warm white, shuffle valid cell indexes, and place one red, one blue, and one yellow accent to guarantee restraint and variety.

steps.title: Render declaratively
steps.explanation: Map the generated cells to stable grid children and change the seed only on initial load or when the labeled regenerate button is pressed.

solutionTracks.explanation: CSS Grid handles the MVP’s geometry: positive tracks cover the surface, gaps form consistent lines, and cells cannot overlap. The TypeScript generator produces only track weights and color assignments, keeping visual policy testable and React rendering small. Later additions can include row or column spans, palette periods, line weights, or composition scoring while preserving the boundary between generation and rendering.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with a recognizable, randomized, responsive result, explicit visual scope, and browser-native constraints that prevent invalid geometry. It is quick to build and readable under interview pressure, with stable randomness, a sparse palette, and a generator that can evolve without direct DOM manipulation. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: Independent grid cells make the first version read more like a structured mosaic than paintings with selectively merged regions.
One grid-wide gap produces a single line weight; historically inspired variation would require extra metadata or layered lines.
Fractional tracks are excellent for responsiveness but less convenient than SVG coordinates for exact export or geometry inspection.
Guaranteeing one of each accent is visually reliable but less organic than a richer composition-scoring policy.

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Rectangular Subdivision
solutionTracks.summary: Recursively split a normalized rectangle, then render the resulting leaf regions as absolutely positioned React elements.

steps.title: Define normalized geometry
steps.explanation: Represent every region as x, y, width, and height percentages so the model is renderer-independent and automatically responsive.

steps.title: Choose bounded splits
steps.explanation: Split between 34% and 66% of the parent and stop by depth, probability, or minimum projected size so no leaf becomes unusable.

steps.title: Bias the orientation
steps.explanation: Prefer vertical splits for wide rectangles and horizontal splits for tall rectangles, using randomness mainly when the aspect ratio is ambiguous.

steps.title: Assign sparse accents
steps.explanation: Generate neutral leaves first, shuffle sufficiently large leaves, and assign the three primary accents to avoid coloring tiny fragments.

steps.title: Project leaves into the DOM
steps.explanation: Render leaf rectangles with percentage positioning and consistent outlines while keeping the recursive algorithm entirely outside JSX.

solutionTracks.explanation: Binary space partitioning models the composition as a tree of split decisions. Each split preserves its parent boundary, so leaves cover the original rectangle without gaps or overlap. Orientation based on aspect ratio and bounded cuts prevent most slivers; depth and probability limits guarantee finite work. Internal nodes can later carry line weights, locked axes, merge decisions, or composition scores without changing the React renderer.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with a richer model that remains manageable during an interview. Children exactly partition their parent, so each split’s correctness can be checked locally. It produces more varied region sizes than a uniform grid, constrains randomness, preserves repeatability, and makes deferred composition rules explicit outside CSS. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: Absolute-positioned leaves need careful outline treatment because adjacent borders can visually double or reveal subpixel seams.
A binary split tree cannot directly create every possible grid topology without later merging or cross-branch alignment rules.
Recursive code is conceptually richer than the CSS Grid MVP and may be harder to explain if interview time is very short.
Percentage rounding is responsive but can create tiny visual seams at some device pixel ratios.

complexity.space: O(number of leaf regions + recursion depth)

solutionTracks.title: Responsive SVG Geometry
solutionTracks.summary: Generate normalized cut coordinates and render fills first, then crisp structural lines in a responsive SVG viewBox.

steps.title: Choose a normalized coordinate system
steps.explanation: Use a 100 by 75 viewBox so the generator works in stable units while the browser scales the final SVG responsively.

steps.title: Generate minimum-safe cuts
steps.explanation: Produce positive weighted segments and normalize their cumulative positions, guaranteeing complete coverage and avoiding nearly coincident random coordinates.

steps.title: Build cells from adjacent cuts
steps.explanation: Every neighboring x and y pair defines one valid non-overlapping rectangle whose width and height are positive by construction.

steps.title: Assign controlled color
steps.explanation: Leave the field neutral and place exactly three shuffled accents, keeping color policy independent from coordinate generation.

steps.title: Draw structure last
steps.explanation: Render colored rectangles before the horizontal and vertical line elements so joins remain crisp and line thickness stays visually consistent.

solutionTracks.explanation: SVG maps the geometry directly to pixels. Normalizing weighted segments produces sorted cuts that cover the viewBox and form valid rectangles. Separate fill and line layers avoid doubled borders and support additional line rules. The geometry can be unit tested, serialized, downloaded, animated, or scored without layout measurements. The viewBox handles responsive scaling.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with precise invariants and a concise browser-native renderer. It separates geometry, palette, and drawing order, produces stable seeded output, scales across devices, and offers the most direct path to export or advanced line rules. Explain the additional SVG concepts within the agreed MVP scope. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: SVG introduces coordinate and drawing-order concepts that may be more machinery than a CSS-only MVP needs.
A full row-by-column cut model remains grid-like until later logic merges cells or terminates selected lines early.
Very thick responsive strokes may need vector-effect or breakpoint tuning if exact screen-space thickness matters.
Large compositions would create many SVG nodes, although the interview-sized region count is comfortably small.

solutionTracks.title: Dijkstra With Priority Queue
solutionTracks.summary: For non-negative road weights, always expand the currently cheapest city and relax outgoing roads.

steps.title: Seed the start
steps.explanation: Distance to the start is zero and all other distances are initially unknown.

steps.title: Expand cheapest candidate
steps.explanation: A priority queue returns the unprocessed node with the smallest known distance.

steps.title: Relax edges
steps.explanation: If reaching a neighbor through the current node is cheaper, update its distance and push it into the queue.

solutionTracks.explanation: With non-negative weights, the first time a node is popped with its best distance, no future path can improve it. The priority queue enforces that safe processing order.

complexity.time: O((V + E) log(E + 2)), including stale priority-queue records

solutionTracks.title: Bellman–Ford Relaxation
solutionTracks.summary: Use repeated edge relaxation as a simple weighted baseline.

steps.title: Initialize distances
steps.explanation: Start is zero; all other nodes are unreachable.

steps.title: Relax every edge
steps.explanation: For at most V−1 passes, improve the target distance with distance[source] + weight.

steps.title: Stop and report
steps.explanation: Stop on an unchanged pass; return −1 if the requested target is still unreachable.

solutionTracks.explanation: After pass i, all paths with at most i edges have been considered. A shortest path without a negative cycle can be chosen simple and uses at most V−1 edges. Stop early when no distance improves. For this prompt weights are non-negative; BFS would be valid only when all edges have equal weight.

questions.title: Meeting Rooms II
questions.summary: Find the minimum number of rooms needed for overlapping meetings.
questions.prompt: Given meeting start and end times, return the minimum number of rooms required so every meeting can be scheduled.

examples.explanation: The first meeting overlaps each shorter meeting.

constraints: A meeting ending at time t frees the room for another meeting starting at t.
Intervals have positive duration: start < end.

solutionTracks.title: End Time Min Heap
solutionTracks.summary: Sort meetings by start time and keep a min heap of room end times to reuse rooms as soon as they free up.

steps.title: Sort starts
steps.explanation: Processing meetings chronologically lets each meeting decide whether the earliest room is already free.

steps.title: Pop free room
steps.explanation: If the smallest end time is at or before the next start, that room can be reused.

steps.title: Track heap size
steps.explanation: After adding the current end, the maximum heap size is the number of rooms required.

solutionTracks.explanation: The heap contains one next-available time per allocated room. A start can reuse the room with the earliest end; otherwise allocate a new room. Only one room needs to be reused per meeting. The heap size never decreases across iterations and equals the maximum rooms allocated. These examples sort the supplied interval array in place.

solutionTracks.title: Separate Start And End Sweep
solutionTracks.summary: Sort starts and ends independently and count simultaneous active meetings as pointers move forward.

steps.title: Sort starts and ends
steps.explanation: The next start adds a room unless the earliest end has already freed one.

steps.title: Move end pointer on reuse
steps.explanation: If a meeting ended before the next start, consume that end and reuse the room.

steps.title: Count active rooms
steps.explanation: Each unreused start increases the number of active rooms and updates the maximum.

solutionTracks.explanation: The sweep compares the next meeting arrival against the earliest departure. That is enough to know whether total concurrent meetings grows or one room is reused.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def min_rooms_sweep(intervals):
    starts = sorted(start for start, end in intervals)
    ends = sorted(end for start, end in intervals)
    used = best = end_i = 0
    for start in starts:
        if start >= ends[end_i]:
            used -= 1
            end_i += 1
        used += 1
        best = max(best, used)
    return best

questions.title: Connected Regions
questions.summary: Count groups of connected land cells in a grid.
questions.prompt: Given a binary grid where 1 is land and 0 is water, return the number of connected land regions using four-direction adjacency.

examples.explanation: The top-left cluster, bottom-left cell, and bottom-right cell are separate.

constraints: Use four-direction adjacency unless the prompt says diagonal connections count.
Input is a nonempty rectangular grid.

solutionTracks.title: Grid DFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Treat each land cell as part of a graph and flood-fill every unseen connected component.

steps.title: Scan every cell
steps.explanation: A new region starts whenever the scan finds land that has not been visited.

steps.title: Flood neighbors
steps.explanation: DFS marks the current cell and recursively explores its four adjacent land neighbors.

steps.title: Count components
steps.explanation: Increment the region count once before each flood-fill because that fill consumes exactly one component.

solutionTracks.explanation: Connectivity is transitive: every land cell reached by the flood fill belongs to the same region. Starting a fill only from unseen land counts each region once.

solutionTracks.title: Union Find Components
solutionTracks.summary: Give every land cell an id, union adjacent land cells, and count unique component roots.

steps.title: Create ids for land
steps.explanation: Map each land coordinate to a disjoint-set id and ignore water cells.

steps.title: Union neighbors
steps.explanation: For each land cell, union it with right and down land neighbors to connect components.

steps.title: Count roots
steps.explanation: After all unions, the number of distinct roots among land ids is the number of regions.

solutionTracks.explanation: Union find stores connected components explicitly. Unioning adjacent land cells merges exactly the cells that share a region, and final roots identify distinct regions. This compact implementation uses path compression without union by rank/size. Do not claim the inverse-Ackermann bound for it. Add union by size to obtain the usual near-linear amortized bound; recursive find can otherwise be deep.

complexity.time: O(N²) conservative worst-case bound, N = rows × columns
